speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OP LEGISLATION RESPECTING HUMANE METHODS OF SLAUGHTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, later this morning I shall be introducing a bill to amend the Criminal Code with regard to the humane slaughtering of food animals. It is the intention to give this bill first reading only and I should like to make a statement now to advise the house of our plans.
For some time there has been a growing demand for action that would compel the slaughterers of food animals to adopt a humane method of killing. The concern has been mainly that these animals are subjected to shackling, hoisting, bleeding, or other processes connected with slaughtering while they are still fully conscious. Special humane slaughter associations have been formed and these, together with the various branches of the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, have spearheaded the drive for legislation to make humane methods of slaughter mandatory.
The previous government took the position that no further legislation was necessary; that the present section 387 of the Criminal Code makes it an offence to cause unnecessary pain and suffering to an animal, and that all that was required was enforcement of this legislation. However, a test case involving the usual slaughter methods in an abattoir came before a magistrate in Vancouver this fall and was dismissed. The decision was appealed, but the appeal was also dismissed. This demonstrated pretty conclusively that something more is required, and we are prepared to act accordingly.
There are difficulties in this field which all have recognized. There are questions as to what type of action or legislation is called for by the government, and at what level of government, and whether a method or methods of humane slaughter exist which it would be sound, from a practical and economic point of view, to require the slaughterers to follow.
A special committee was formed in the province of Ontario to study these problems,
including representatives from the meat packers' council of Canada and the Ontario
S.P.C.A. The government made available two of its experts in the field, and more recently the national research council has joined in a full-scale investigation program.
The government welcomed the formation of this committee and looked forward to its advice. We were concerned to avoid action which would produce legislation which would either be simply unenforced and unenforceable or, alternatively, if enforced would simply result in driving a number of packers out of business. At the suggestion of the committee action was accordingly deferred until they might have an opportunity to report.
An interim report was received from the committee on October 31, and on November 13 my colleague the Minister of Agriculture and I, together with our parliamentary assistants and departmental officers, met with the joint chairmen and other representatives of the committee.
At that meeting we were advised that while no complete solution to the problem of method so far as hogs and sheep are concerned had been agreed upon as being immediately practicable for universal action in Canada, nevertheless such methods do exist. We were also advised that there was agreement that humane methods of slaughter of cattle could immediately be enforced. It was also clear that the committee felt that action by government is essential.
The committee is to continue its study on the same basis as before, with the full assistance of the government experts and the national research council. In this connection I find that I must make a correction in a statement I made on December 10. It was my understanding as a result of that meeting, that the S.P.C.A. representatives felt there was nothing further they could usefully do, having made clear their views as to the necessity for legislation. I am glad to find that they are continuing as members of the committee, and that the committee is functioning fully.
There is, then, general agreement that humane methods of slaughter exist and can be made applicable in Canada although there are still some problems to be solved. In considering our course of action we have had to bear the following factors in mind. First,

Ministerial Statements that there is a measure of divided responsibility, and that in any criminal legislation to be introduced we must bear in mind that the responsibility for enforcement rests with the provinces. Second, that hasty action on the part of the government might force out of business abattoirs and packing plants and could result in a shortage of such commodities as bacon, etc. Third, that impracticable or unenforceable legislation does more harm than good. Fourth, that the provinces have an interest in the matter especially from the point of view of enforcement, and therefore should be consulted.
We have accordingly drafted a bill which we believe to be practical and enforceable, first reading of which I shall be moving in a few moments. It is not the intention to proceed further with the bill at this session, but to make it available to all interested persons, including especially the attorneys general of the provinces. We shall welcome their views and suggestions as to the legislation, and also the views and suggestions of the packers and all those interested or involved in this problem.
All representations received will then be studied, and we shall be prepared to make such changes in the legislation as appear desirable in the light of those studies. After making such changes as are necessary we would propose to reintroduce and enact the legislation at the next session of parliament.
In this way we will hope to have sound legislation which will produce the desired result with a minimum of hardship and a maximum of co-operation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre asked why the work program announced by the Canadian National Railways did not include some special projects for Fort Rouge and Trans-cona.
The car equipment program that is being undertaken by the Canadian National Railways is the conversion of damaged or obsolete cars into extra gang feeding cars, bunk cars, and so forth. This work can only be done in regularly equipped car shops. In the case of Fort Rouge, as the hon. member knows, the car shops at that point were destroyed by fire two years ago. With regard to Trans-cona, a special work program on hopper and general service cars is already under way there.
I might advise the house that I have asked the management of the Canadian National Railways to make a careful review of possible work projects that might be put into effect at other points on the system, and they have assured me they will do so.
Also, yesterday the hon. member for St. Antoine-Westmount inquired if it is the intention of the railway to proceed more rapidly with the work at Cote de Liesse and other points in the Montreal area.
As he knows, a contract has been let for grading at Cote de Liesse, and the management advise me that this work is well in hand and they do not think it could be further expedited. With regard to other points in the Montreal area, as I have just mentioned in reply to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, the management have indicated they will give earnest consideration to expanding the work program wherever that is possible.
The hon. member for Essex East asked yesterday if the work program planned for Windsor airport could be expedited. Certain additional runway work is contemplated for the airport next year, and my officials are presently reviewing the project to see whether a start could be made this winter. The problem is one of getting the engineering

plans ready, and every effort will be made to expedite the project, although it is not yet possible to say exactly how soon tenders may be called.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CIGARETTES-INQUIRY AS TO LOSS LEADER SELLING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, although it is ordinarily not the practice to disclose whether inquiries are going on in any particular trade or industry unless and until a report is made and published, nevertheless since no particular part

of the business community is identified in the question just asked I can say that the combines branch has lately received a considerable number of complaints about the loss leader selling of cigarettes with injurious effects on small businesses. Inquiries are accordingly being pursued under section 412 of the Criminal Code. This section provides in part that it is an offence to engage in a policy of selling goods at prices unreasonably low, having or designed to have the effect of substantially lessening competition or eliminating a competitor. The inquiry will be pursued vigorously.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DISA3LED PERSONS STATEMENT ON AMENDMENT OF REGULATIONS UNDER ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre asked me whether or not the regulations pertaining to the Disabled Persons Act had been amended since the revision of this measure at the current session of parliament.
In answer, I would inform the hon. member that a number of changes had to be made in the disability allowance regulations consequent upon the amendments to the act approved by parliament last month. For example, changes in the legislation with respect to the eligibility of certain patients in certain types of institutions require some follow-up by way of alterations in the regulations covering this same matter. These changes are under consideration at the present time, and when drafts are ready the provincial authorities will be consulted with regard to them. As soon as there is general agreement on the text of proposed changes in the regulations these will be put forward for approval by the governor in council. I expect that this will be done early in the new year.
I might add, Mr. Speaker, that I have not forgotten the undertaking I gave at the time of the debate on the Disabled Persons Act to carry out a comprehensive review of the regulations as soon as possible. For reasons which the hon. member will, I am sure, appreciate, I have not yet been able to complete this task, but I shall follow up what I said during the debate at the earliest possible opportunity.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words at this time. First of all I should like to take advantage of this opportunity to say what I am sure the minister has learned by this time, that the Department of National Health and Welfare is indeed manned by a distinguished group of public servants from the deputy minister level down to the lower grade workers. As one who was minister of the department for almost 11 years I thought I should like to take this opportunity to pay a tribute to the personnel of the Department of Health and Welfare who made my task an agreeable one; a task, I think, that produced some very constructive results.
The Acting Prime Minister said the other day that Canada had reason to be proud of its public servants. I am sure all of us in every quarter of the house will agree with that observation, and I want to say in particular that the public servants of the Department of National Health and Welfare are ladies and gentlemen who have served and are serving the country with distinction and the people of the Canada have every reason to be proud of them. As the former minister I want to say in the house that I have special reason to be grateful for the loyalty and service which they gave to Canada and to the department during my tenure of office.
I am wondering whether or not it is the minister's intention to indicate at some stage the extent to which it has been possible for him to cut down the expenditures of the department, in accordance with the statements made during the course of the election campaign by hon. gentlemen opposite. I recognize, of course, that the expenditures of the Department of National Health and Welfare are by no means all controllable, but there are areas where, if an administration wanted to, that could be done. I do not know whether or not the minister will indicate whether he has been able to effect the kind of savings which it was suggested, not with regard to any particular department but with regard to the government generally, would be effected by the administration of which he is now a member. We shall look forward to hearing from him in that particular later on.
I want to take advantage on the first item to again express what I believe is a wide measure of regret in this country at the failure of the government to give evidence

Supply-Health and Welfare of any progress in the implementation of the federal government's share of responsibility under the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act. This matter has been referred to by interrogation in the house and by statements made by some hon. members from time to time, but I think the minister will agree that anything I have said, certainly anything involving him personally, cannot be characterized as having been anything but responsible and fair. However, I find it necessary now to say that as we come to the period of adjournment, after many days of discussion in parliament since October 14, there is a wide measure of regret at the lack of evidence of progress being made by this government in respect of this particular matter.
In reply the hon. gentleman may say that as a result of the discussions at the dominion-provincial conference my statement cannot be fully substantiated. In that context I think it must be realized what took place at the dominion-provincial conference. The Prime Minister at that conference said-although he had refused to say so on the Friday before the conference in this house-that the federal government was prepared to include tuberculosis and mental illness under the terms of the hospital insurance act. He noted that this was in conformity with assurances he himself had given during the course of the election campaign and assurances that had been given by implication as a result of the stand taken by hon. gentlemen opposite when they were in opposition.
The fact is that these promises are not being kept by the government in its stated policy. The Prime Minister said the federal government was prepared to include tuberculosis and mental illness but that the costs involved would be deducted from any increase made in further fiscal grants to the provinces. That statement is not in conformity with the promises made during the election campaign. That is not the kind of urging that was made of the previous government by hon. gentlemen opposite when they were in the opposition. The result will be -and I am now giving my warning to the minister-that certainly two provinces, namely the province of Ontario and the province of Quebec, will want to get their full fiscal grants under the new arrangement. Then in subsequent years, having received those moneys, they will come to the administration and seek to get compensation with regard to tuberculosis and mental illness. I am sure the minister will be aware of that danger. I am sure it is a likely development as a result of the changed position which the government has taken in this matter.


My reason for expressing regret again is that the minister, in answer to questions, has not revealed that any negotiations whatsoever have taken place between the government and the provincial governments in the matter of the implementation of the hospital insurance act. The minister has said on occasion that his officials are available, and we know that recently there was a technical conference on the public services level. However, I am sure the only way in which to make progress in a matter of this sort is for these negotiations to be initiated and carried on by the minister himself. Officials in government departments can go only so far. They must always have their conduct tempered by considerations of government policy. The only way in which you can have any advance made in a matter of this sort is by a vigorous interest on the part of the minister concerned and on the part of the government as a whole.
In this context I ask the minister this question. Apart from his meetings at the dominion-provincial conference, can he tell the house what negotiations he has carried on with any provincial government in trying to encourage the latter to take steps by which this measure can be implemented at the earliest possible date? I find it difficult to understand why, at this late date, there are no agreements whatsoever with any of the provinces. I cannot understand why there are no agreements signed now with the provinces of Saskatchewan and British Columbia, provinces that now have schemes in being. If the minister wants to give the country the impression that there has been no dilatoriness on his part or on the part of the administration, I think he will have to explain why no agreements have yet been concluded with at least these two provinces in which hospital insurance is in existence.
Prior to the election on June 10 the situation was that all the provinces that had expressed their willingness to come within the four corners of the federal scheme had been sent a draft master agreement. My recollection is that not only had that agreement been sent to the provinces of British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Prince Edward Island, Newfoundland and Ontario but that as well, in order to facilitate matters, we had sent the agreement to the provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, two provinces that had given evidence of rather intensive interest in the possibility of an agreement with the federal government.
What has happened? What reaction have we had from the provinces with regard to these agreements? Why has no agreement

been signed yet, for instance, with the province of Ontario? In the month of April we met with the government of the province of Ontario and I indicated, on behalf of the government of the day, that if by the end of September we had not concluded agreements with any of the provinces we would have to give consideration to arrangements which would place the province of Ontario in a position where it could begin its scheme without any concern over the failure of other provinces to participate. speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON RETURN FROM CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would first like to thank the house for granting me the right at this time, by their indulgence, to say a few

NATO-Paris Conference reports on everything we do, similar to the practice followed in all other NATO military commands.
Now I come to the question that was raised in the house in connection with economic developments. To a surprising degree, I thought, having regard to the experience of the last few years, it was reiterated over and over again that NATO is more than a military alliance; that it is a community whose members are guided by similar fundamental ideas, and that under article II of the treaty we have agreed to give effect to the community by co-operation and collaboration in the important aspects of international relations.
At the meeting this week the flowering of this concept of the Atlantic community was much in evidence. There was not a great deal of divergence of view as to the necessity of greater and more expanding developments in connection with the article in question. Indeed, the wording of the communique itself indicates the degree to which, almost for the first time, the nations comprising the alliance were in agreement when they pledged themselves to this effect; that "they will cooperate among themselves and with other free governments to further the achievement of economic stability, a steady rate of economic growth, and the expansion of international trade through the further reduction of exchange and trade barriers."
Then there was a reference that I think I should mention at this moment. They reaffirmed the desirability of a closer economic association with the countries of western Europe, which they deemed to be in the interest of all countries and which will lend encouragement to the successful development of the European economic community and the European free trade area. In connection with the latter, when this matter came before the council I used the following words in order to clarify and make certain Canada's stand in this regard:
When the proposal for the European free trade area was placed before the Canadian government for consideration it qualified its approval by specifically excluding from its scope food, drink and tobacco. By this exclusion the trading interests of Canada were protected, and on this qualified basis the Canadian government has been able to give its approval to the proposal.
I would have preferred to have had this omitted from the communique, or alternatively to spell out the nature of our reservation. However, recognizing the strong desire of a number of governments represented here to include a brief endorsement along the lines of the draft before us, I am not going to press our objection.
We did repeat for the record that Canada's approval of the European free trade area depends on the exclusion of the three groups of products to which I have already referred,
[Mr. Diefenbaker.l
the exclusion from the ambit of the proposals of the commodities in question.
I come now to one other matter that has been foremost in recent weeks, particularly in connection with the shipment of small amounts of arms to Tunis and the strong objection taken by the government of France to the course of action followed in that regard, which underlined the necessity of there being the closest consultation among all the members before action is taken. That was one of the most striking general matters at this conference, the determination of all the partners to develop still further the habit of consultation, which is an essential element in maintaining the cohesion and unity of the alliance. The Canadian delegation stressed the importance of the habit of consultation, the neighbourly frame of mind, and the desirability of member nations refraining from adopting firm policy stands or making major political announcements on questions that affect the interests of their NATO partners until they have consulted with them.
I am convinced that this habit, this frame of mind, will still further develop interdependence. Certainly there was unanimous support in this regard among all the members present. It was recognized, too, that since the aim of the Soviet bloc was to weaken and disrupt the western world by all the means at its disposal, the alliance could not be concerned only with the north Atlantic area and the military defence of that area. It was agreed that our political and economic strength must be organized on the principle of interdependence.
However, this does not imply, and the Canadian delegation made that very clear during the discussions, an extension of the commitment of the alliance to defend other areas, nor does it imply in any way a desire on the part of NATO to interfere in the affairs of other countries. Our interest was to affirm the support of our governments for the independence and sovereignty of states in areas such as the Middle East, and our continuing interest in the economic wellbeing of their peoples. To the many nations which have gained their independence since the end of the second world war and to all other peoples who are dedicated to peace and freedom, the NATO countries offered their co-operation on a basis of complete equality and in a spirit of fraternity.
I stated in the house before the Canadian delegation left for Paris that the government felt that particular attention should be given at the NATO meeting to the implementation of the objectives set forth in article 2. I stressed this view in Paris, with particular reference for the need of members of the

alliance to bear in mind the needs of the underdeveloped nations. I said the free world would not accept a situation where half mankind is well fed and the other half is not. Such a situation merely invites communist mischief.
In this connection I said that something in the nature of a NATO food bank might be created to make food available to countries which are in need and which are in danger of being overrun and subverted by the Soviet union. It would also make possible the availability of those deposits of food in the event of war. It is our hope that such an eventuality will not occur, and that we have come a long way in the last few days toward once more reinforcing the forces of peace.
In connection with scientific and technical matters within the alliance there was a general recognition of the need to increase the number of trained scientists and technicians in most of the countries. In Canada, as elsewhere, progress in this field will depend not only on the state contribution but also on the devoted contribution of teachers and scientists in our schools and universities. It will also depend on the support which governments will give to institutions which provide courses in scientific subjects, and this government intends shortly to give full reconsideration to its policy in this regard and have it placed before parliament.
To give effect to a co-operative effort within the alliance it was decided to arrange a NATO science committee on which all member countries will be represented by men qualified to speak authoritatively on scientific policy, and to appoint a scientific adviser to the secretary general of NATO. While some may say these were merely procedural decisions, none the less we had before us specific proposals for developing co-operation in this field between NATO countries which will be worked out in detail by qualified authorities on the new committee.
Let me mention one other matter. We thought of the people behind the iron curtain, people who believe in freedom as we do. Sometimes we are apt to forget them. When the declaration was being drafted I had the honour to move that there should be the inclusion of a paragraph to give to those people, whether in the Ukraine, in Hungary, in Poland, in East Germany, in the Balkan states, or in any other countries, the hope that the day will come when they will be able to live in freedom; to let them realize that we have not forgotten and do not forget their heroism and their plight. We want them to know that the flickering flame of freedom they have kept alive is being seen by those
NATO-Paris Conference who represent countries under democratic control. It was accepted that this paragraph should be included in order to give some hope to those who live in the expectation that tomorrow may give them new opportunities in life and the right of human beings to enjoy a measure of freedom. The portion in question is as follows:
For the entire world it is both a tragedy and a great danger that the peoples under international communist rule-their national independence, human liberties and their standard of living as well as their scientific and technological achievements- have been sacrificed to the purposes of world domination and military power. The suppression of their liberty will not last forever. Already in these countries there is evidence of the growing desire for intellectual and economic freedom. If the free nations are steadfast the totalitarian menace that now confronts them will eventually recede.
While I was in Paris I was met by a group of 15 to 20 representatives of those peoples behind the iron curtain, who asked for nothing in the nature of a declaration belligerent in its wording. All they asked for was a word of appreciation so the aspirations and hopes of those people will be maintained.
That in general, sir, represents a summary of the principles that activated those who met there. In brief the alliance, I believe, has made a substantive contribution to the cause of peace, not only by reaffirming its purely defensive character-that was underlined and re-emphasized over and over again-but also by leaving the door open to meaningful disarmament negotiations. Decisions have been taken which, through a closer integration of our individual forces, will result in the strengthening of the alliance and I believe will ensure greater security to our peoples.
The machinery of NATO will be adapted to make possible the full use of the resources of each and all of the member nations. Above everything else a new impetus has been given at the highest possible level and a revised vision to our alliance which will help us to translate its aims and objectives into practical achievements. While there may be those who feel otherwise, one of the most moving things that took place at that conference was at its conclusion, when the President of the United States asked that the leaders of the various countries should engage in silent prayer for the welfare and the preservation of freedom in mankind.
I am not going to say more than that; but never have I seen a group of men less actuated by any purpose other than to achieve, or to lay the foundations for, peace, and so to act that the 450 million people whom they represented will at least know that everything has been done and everything will be done to ensure through negotiation the maintenance of our way of life; that we are prepared, not

NATO-Paris Conference in a spirit of appeasement but with a realization of the awful realities that face us, to go as far as possible to bring about that climate and that atmosphere which will ensure the laying of the foundation, internationally, of peace through disarmament.
Each member government will now have to review either individually or in the council the implications of the practical steps that have been taken. Each of us-and I speak personally when I say this-endeavoured to express the view of the Canadian people and to make some contribution to the development of that sense of partnership with our immediate allies which has been so necessary in recent days. No one who was there could countenance the thought that we shall not succeed, for we must.
I know what the cynics will say. They have done it all down through the ages. They will contend that the declaration and the communique are simply the same old tired cliches strung together in a different arrangement but leaving the old patterns substantially unchanged. That is not so. This conference has taken striking decisions that affect the military posture, the scientific disposition, and a new and imaginative economic approach that have both domestic and external applications to all the 15 countries. We have extended the range of our concern where economic and social matters are involved to take in underdeveloped countries outside and beyond our alliance.
These to me are significant and profound advances in the NATO of today; and I hope, sir, that what has been done will render NATO perceptibly more united, actually more united, more effective, and with a more revived purpose than was the case one week ago today.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON RETURN FROM CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure we have all listened with great interest to this summary report by the Prime Minister of Canada with respect to the important meeting of the heads of the governments of the countries that make up the north Atlantic treaty organization, and that no one would wish either to underestimate or, on the other hand, to exaggerate the practical results of these deliberations.
There is no doubt that there is something of value in having had the heads of the governments participate in the communique that was issued and in which their unity about the objectives of the alliance is once more very clearly asserted, perhaps asserted with even more clarity and certainly with more specific developments than were included even in the treaty that was signed. But as in all other human endeavours it is not

sufficient to state objectives and do what might be the implementation of wishful thinking. What is necessary is to have achievements expressed not only in words, however necessary that is in the first instance, but by actual conduct that gives effect to the expressions found in those words.
Everything that is said in the communique and everything we have had in the interesting report given to us by the Prime Minister was expressed in general terms contained implicitly in the treaty itself, and has been expressed in diplomatic exchanges many times since. I think we have reason to feel that the cost to us and to our people, to all who belong to the north Atlantic treaty organization, great as it has been has been a cost that provided in return to our peoples value for the whole of it.
It is now nine years that the alliance has been in existence and has been pursuing its objectives. As the Prime Minister pointed out, during that time there has been no further expansion of the domination of one great power over its neighbouring countries. That was the thing against which the participants in the alliance wished to guard when the treaty was originally signed. Everyone accepted the language of the treaty, and I would imagine that all the member nations feel that their respective governments have endeavoured to give effect to the undertakings of the various clauses. But although the objectives have been the same for all of us, the extent to which the conduct of the 15 nations has been directed at realizing those objectives has not been completely satisfactory to every one of the nations forming the alliance.
With respect, for instance, to the matter of economic collaboration, I am sure all the governments wish to have the other members of the alliance in a satisfactory economic position. But more could have been done than has been done to strengthen the economies of the participant nations. Now that attention has been called to the matter again in this solemn pronouncement by the heads of the governments who attended the recent meeting we will hope there will be an increase in the effectiveness of the economic collaboration that is necessary to maintain our standards of living, and at the same time feel that we are doing everything it is proper to do to maintain that defensive strength that will permit the alliance to realize the general objective for which we have been striving.
We note that the Prime Minister says we should all feel that everything that can be done by negotiation to give greater assurance

NATO-Paris Conference
to the foundations of peace in the world is being done and will continue to be done and that, in spite of what we cannot all look upon as universal good will, we will continue to hope that there will be achievements that will be substantial. I am sure those of us who heard over the radio this morning that Mr. Gromyko had declared that Russia could not participate in a conference at the level of ministers of external affairs shuddered somewhat at that early pronouncement. We do hope we will be able to convince them that we are sincere in our desire to treat with them on a basis of national equality in regard to the objective which is and must be of as great interest to them as it is to us, or at least to their people as it is to our people.
I suppose in order to make progress all of us, each and every one, who have any influence whatsoever on the conduct of ourselves and our fellow citizens, should endeavour to bring ourselves to the frame of mind in which we can attempt to negotiate with some feeling that there could be decisions arrived at that would be kept which would enable us to protect our own and future generations against the catastrophic consequences that will be inevitable if we cannot reach some satisfactory arrangements -arrangements we will not have to call appeasement, but that will at least appease the anxieties that must somewhat becloud the frame of mind we endeavour to reach at this season of the year.
Whether it be brought about by silent prayer, as the head of the great American nation requested at the close of the conference, or otherwise, I think there is a necessity perhaps on both sides of a more confident approach to the possibilities of reaching some kind of an arrangement that will be the result of negotiating from strength, but not forgetting that there is strength on both sides and that that strength would be disastrous to both sides as soon as unleashed by either one or the other.
We are coming to the anniversary of that event which was heralded to the world by the declaration that peace was being brought to men of good will. I think the men who attended this top level meeting of the north Atlantic treaty organization were all men of good will. I hope their good will will be recognized. It is sometimes necessary, without being disposed to resort to anything to which the term "appeasement" in the unacceptable sense could be applied, to express a genuine, confident desire to conduct negotiations on the basis of it being possible that they will succeed. It is in that spirit that I
think we should, in our silent prayers, accept this heralding of the coming of peace to men of good will in this world.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON RETURN FROM CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it is well that the Prime Minister should have taken the earliest opportunity to come before the house and give us a report on the extremely important conference from which he has just come.
I think there are times when an atmosphere is felt. As I listened, particularly to the Leader of the Opposition, whose words I think were well chosen and who expressed the thoughts of many of us as we listened to him, I thought that this morning we have such an atmosphere. I do not think there is an individual anywhere who is not impressed with the dangers that surround us and beset the world. I think we all looked to this great conference which has just concluded in Paris in the hope that something concrete might come of it, something that would give us hope for the future.
As I listened to the Prime Minister this morning my heart sank, because I could find nothing concrete that gave us any hope of peace. There is to be co-ordination of defence, co-ordination of defence production, but no co-ordination for economic integration among the nations comprising the north Atlantic treaty organization which was envisaged nine years ago when article 11 was adopted by the nations which now compose the north Atlantic alliance.
I should like to know what the Prime Minister had in his mind in concrete terms when he mentioned economic aid at the NATO conference, but perhaps that may come when we reassemble after Christmas. However, I think this statement, in the light of the documents that may be issued and what we may know at that time, should be the basis for a debate on external affairs so that we may have more than a few moments in which to discuss this extremely important matter.
Then we have the proposal for a conference of the scientists of the NATO countries. What for? To improve our weapons of war, to make further preparation for defence. That may be necessary in the world in which we live, but as I said on a former occasion, why can we not go beyond that? Why cannot Canada say that we would welcome within our borders a scientific conference representing scientists of all the nations of the world, so that others than statesmen may discuss these problems and guide the world toward some peaceful solutions? I welcome the suggestion that there should be negotiation but, like the Leader of the Opposition, I believe it must be negotiation with a large measure of good will.

NATO-Paris Conference
If I may stray outside of our own parliament, may I say that I read with a good deal of misgiving an article by the secretary of state for the United States as well as some of his statements just prior to this conference. How can you expect negotiation to be successful when the spokesman for the most powerful nation within NATO makes the kind of statements which one heard and which one read in the current issue of Life magazine? I think we need a new approach, and I think particularly we need a new approach among the most powerful of the nations on both sides.
I read the Bulganin letter with a great deal of care. I do not think this letter has been considered or answered by NATO. I think it is a letter which should be answered paragraph by paragraph and sentence by sentence, and if no one else would undertake it, I would say our own Secretary of State for External Affairs should undertake the writing of such a document. Because I believe, when we contrast the report of the Prime Minister this morning respecting the NATO conference and Mr. Dulles' statement with the Bulganin letter, that once again we are losing the battle of propaganda.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON RETURN FROM CONFERENCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON RETURN FROM CONFERENCE
speechtext:
This is a struggle for men's minds if ever there was a struggle for anything. We exclude 600 million people because we refuse to recognize that there is a government in China. Yet we are engaged in a struggle, a desperate struggle for men's minds. Through the years I have felt that we have given some of the choicest weapons in that field to the other side.
I feel we need a new approach, and I would like to know what are the concrete proposals for these new approaches. We did not get them this morning. I am anxious to read the documents which will be issued; I am anxious to read what the leaders of other countries have to say in order that I might at least arrive at a clearer understanding of what happened at NATO than I have been able to obtain from the statement of the Prime Minister. It is all very well; the words are fine, the sentiments expressed are good but, as has been pointed out by the Leader of the Opposition, they were generalizations.
So I say to the Prime Minister and to the government that I hope when we reassemble after Christmas we can set aside a day when we may discuss external affairs in the light of the new developments-I have not referred to the new dangers-so that we may make a real appraisal of what happened at NATO and whether there is any cause for hope.

This proposal to put missiles in countries in Europe was, I notice, a bilateral arrangement. I also notice that there is tremendous opposition on the part of some of our most progressive European allies, Norway and Denmark and so on. The Prime Minister said he listened to the debate in the House of Commons in England last night, and no doubt he heard there the speeches of both Mr. Macmillan and the acting leader of the opposition; possibly he also saw the vote taken, one of the narrowest majorities the present government of Britain has received since it took office, with abstentions by some of its own supporters, and possibly also some members voting unwillingly with the government. All this indicates that in the United Kingdom, one of the powerful countries, as well as in the smaller countries, there is misgiving and active opposition as to this proposal to put the new missile weapons in European countries.
If I were a Russian and I lived in the Soviet union I think I would feel just as I would feel as a Canadian living here if I saw all around my country bases with high powered planes in which new weapons of war and guided missiles were being placed for the potential destruction of my country. I cannot see how this helps the cause of peace, but that should be the subject of debate at some other time.
We in this party, in common with others in this house, have supported NATO. We appreciate the achievements which have been made by NATO and we know that what has been said-that NATO has prevented the spread of the influence of the Soviet union through subversive activity since Czechoslovakia-is quite correct. However, are we always going to live under this shadow of war, war that would bring universal destruction and universal annihilation? I want to say that I believe every member of this house-the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition and every one of us sitting in our seats-feels, as the Leader of the Opposition said, particularly at this time of the year when the bells ring out and the message of peace on earth to men of good will is in our minds, that we should see if we cannot bring about measures of good will so that we may negotiate an end to this terrible threat which hangs over us all.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON RETURN FROM CONFERENCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON RETURN FROM CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Over the past week, Mr. Speaker, I believe many Canadians have been keenly interested in the reports which have emanated from Paris. I was particularly interested in the attitude toward the conference and its work expressed by a number of United States reporters. If one is to believe what they wrote, then the

NATO meeting was a flop, because that is the general opinion expressed by so many United States writers. Whether that was because those reporters felt the United States did not have its own way entirely at the conference I could not tell, but certainly there seems to be quite a lot of disappointment that the United States suggestions were not altogether followed at the conference. I am glad they were not.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON RETURN FROM CONFERENCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON RETURN FROM CONFERENCE
speechtext:
I feel the United States did not have a realistic attitude toward this meeting. I am not asking the Prime Minister or his colleagues to corroborate what I have said, but that has been my impression; that they went over with an eye concentrated on one purpose, which was to impress upon European countries the necessity for accepting equipment of the latest type with which to arm the bases which are supposed to make a ring around Russia. For that reason perhaps many people got the idea that the conference was not successful.
I listened most carefully to the sobering report of the Prime Minister this morning. I am glad he came in as quickly as he did, while parliament is still in session and before the Christmas recess, in order to give us this report. I found that what he had to say contained some reassurance although, as I said, it was to me quite sobering. Like the Leader of the Official Opposition I think he chose his words well, but I feel reaffirmation in high sounding terms of the purposes and objectives of NATO is not enough. What we do in the years ahead, and it seems to me more particularly in the months ahead, to translate the important principles adopted by the alliance nine years ago into effective action is going to be the criterion of the success of that alliance.
I do not for one moment mean to imply that we think the alliance has not accomplished much in the nine years it has been in existence. While the cost of Canada's participation in the north Atlantic treaty has been very great, and probably will continue for years to be exeedingly heavy, we think it can be looked upon as a good investment if it has done nothing more in those nine years than prevent further expansion of Godless communism throughout Europe and the western world. We think, however, that the true measure of whether it will continue to be a good investment in the future will depend on how much is done to give practical application to the high-sounding principles that have been expressed as its purposes and objectives.
NATO-Paris Conference
Sabre-rattling is not enough to keep the peace. There are those, perhaps, who believe we have to develop a fighting machine which will be superior to that of our competitors, the Russians especially; but I repeat that in my judgment sabre-rattling does not do very much good compared with quiet preparation for negotiation from strength. There is quite a difference between the two; and while many people may say that the strong proposal of the United States to arm the European bases with nuclear warheads frightens the Russians, let us not overlook the fact that Russia does not make any bones about the 500 submarines she has ranging the seas from which she can launch nuclear weapons against her enemies, making us feel a little insecure as well.
I think we must keep that in mind. Both sides, as the Leader of the Opposition has said, are strong, and we must never overlook that fact. But that must not deter us for one moment from completing our preparations so we can carry on negotiations from strength.
Let me say, Mr. Speaker, that the negotiations are going to be mighty important too, and those negotiations will have to be carried out on a high moral plane. Now is the time, if ever in the history of this world, when the nations composing the NATO alliance should put their cards face upward on the table and in every way carry on their dealings on the highest moral plane. There should be no attempt, it seems to me, to negotiate in such a way as to give people the impression that we are attempting to do as Chamberlain did at Munich back in 1938. I do not think this is a time for appeasement, by any means. It is a time for peace with honour, and I think we can only achieve that if we are strong and at the same time seized with the necessity of treating other peoples in the world as equal to ourselves.
I do not like this idea which is too often abroad that what we people in the western nations have to do is to bring other people up to our level. Bless my soul, some of the people in the east are far beyond us in moral and spiritual achievements, and it seems to me we have to get over to them the idea that we are prepared to meet them as equals and negotiate with them as equals for peace.
I wish to say in conclusion, Mr. Speaker, that I think it is now time the Prime Minister should prepare and deliver to the Canadian people as a whole the kind of report I suggested he should make when I spoke before he left for the NATO meeting. I think the Canadian people want to hear from the Prime Minister the details of what went on at

Supply-Health and Welfare NATO. Reports from this parliament are not carried adequately enough for the people to get a clear idea of what is going on.
I am glad to see the delegation back, looking as well and fit as they do today. It must have been a very heavy task and a difficult time for them, and I hope every single one of us will be preprared to express his views some time after the resumption of the parliamentary session in the New Year on these very important matters which constitute the effort to attain peace. But I cannot help thinking, Mr. Speaker, that if the world is ever going to achieve peace it has to start with the individual, with each one of us here.
I learned years ago from an old Chinese philosopher who said this: "If there is righteousness in the heart, there will be beauty in the character; if there is beauty in the character, there will be happiness in the home; if there is happiness in the home, there will be strength in the nation; if there is strength in the nation, there will be peace in the world."

subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before we interrupted this particular discussion to enable the Prime Minister to make a 

report on the important conference in Paris of the north Atlantic powers I was dealing with the situation that confronts us in the province of Ontario as a result of the fact that at the present time no agreements whatsoever have been concluded between the federal government and the provinces pursuant to the provisions of the Hospital Insurance Act introduced in the previous session of parliament by the government at that time headed by the present Leader of the Opposition.
I had indicated that in a conference I had with the government of the province of Ontario some time during the course of last spring agreed that if agreements had not been concluded by the end of September with the five other consenting provinces other arrangements would have to be made to avoid the very difficult situation which could arise in the province of Ontario in view of the fact that the premier of that province had stated that he proposed to begin his hospital insurance scheme in Ontario on January 1, 1959.
I was about to indicate before the interruption that in connection with the preparation which understandably the government of Ontario must make that that government must be in a position well ahead of the starting date of having clear understandings with the federal government. The province of Ontario and indeed every province could not be expected to start their schemes unless they were assured that the federal government would begin to share in the costs of the operation of the various plans. In the meantime arrangements would have to be made with private insurance groups, with labour organizations and with employer organizations all leading to the situation in which insured people under these various plans could be given some guarantee that they would not be without the benefits of hospital insurance either under government or under private auspices. The only way that a chaotic condition could be avoided would be by dispatch in getting agreements between the two senior levels of government, and every step would have to be taken to make sure that that dangerous possibility did not confront the provinces concerned.
Notwithstanding the announcement made by the government, that if there was a measure of unanimity on the part of the provinces it was prepared to bring in an amendment to provide for sharing of costs by the federal government at a date other than that referred to in the existing legislation there is great danger now in the light of the only evidence that is available to the house and to the country of the possibility of that chaotic

situation arising. I find it difficult indeed to understand why there are not agreements now concluded with at least four of the provinces. I could go further and say that I am sure that if the necessary interest and will existed on the part of the government agreements with the six provinces could by now be concluded.
It is all very well to suggest that the government proposes to meet this situation by amending the act in order to make payments possible, let us say, to the province of Ontario; but the fact is that if the government is going to take that step, and it has announced its decision so to do, I do not know how it will explain with regard to those provinces that now have schemes in being that it has not taken steps already to provide payments to these particular provinces.
It may be said in answer that that was not the policy of the government of which I was a member. That is true, but as I have indicated we did suggest to the province of Ontario that if agreements were not concluded by September other arrangements would have to be made. But there was a good reason for the policy we were pursuing because our objective was to bring in a maximum number of provinces under a system of hospital insurance based on cooperative financial arrangements between the two senior levels of government. It was as a result of our adhering to the formula of six provinces that we were well on our way to something that approximated a nationwide scheme.
However, as a result of the situation that now develops, are we any nearer to such an approximation? Are we any nearer to having any more than the provinces of British Columbia and Saskatchewan, possibly Alberta, and Ontario with schemes of hospital insurance available to their respective constituents? I think we are not. I think that as a result of the failure of this government to conclude agreements certainly by the end of September and as the result of its failure since the end of September to give evidence of progress we are not going to have the nationwide approach we could have had if there had been alacrity and a greater evidence of interest and concern on the part of the administration.
There will be the greatest regret on the part not only of the people of the various provinces but of the people all over the country that such little progress, if any at all, has been made in the matter of hospital insurance. If there was a justification for the decision that parliament took, in the month of April in accepting the federal government's proposal for a system of hospital insurance,
Supply-Health and Welfare I believe this government can be charged with great neglect in the face of the position which parliament then took, in the light of the demand all over this country, for not having marched with a firmer step and with greater dispatch regarding a matter which means so much to the preservation of the health standards of this country and to providing health assistance to the people.
I was a little disturbed the other day when, in answer to a question put by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, the minister replied that it was proposed to continue the health grants introduced by the government of Mr. Mackenzie King in the month of May, 1948, but, since there might be some overlapping, there could in consequence of that be some modification of those grants, or the withdrawing of some of them. The word "withdrawing" is my own and I do not want to do any injustice to the reply of the minister. But he did indicate the possibility that, because of the overlapping, some of those grants would have to be discontinued or some modifications made as a result of the alleged overlapping. If that is done there will be genuine regret in the country. That kind of reply fails to indicate an appreciation of the full reason for those grants. Those grants have nothing whatever to do with hospitalization.

My hon. friend says a "re-allocation". That disturbs me all the more. These grants were introduced in this house as a condition precedent to the day when we would be adopting a form of hospital insurance. Indeed, the prime minister of that day said that these grants were a prerequisite to the setting up of a system of, I think the words he used on that occasion were, health insurance, and that the grants themselves were designed to prepare for the day when we would have the facilities to make hospital insurance a possibility. These grants included assistance for public health, for tuberculosis control, for mental health, for hospital construction, for medical scientific research, for professional training, for rehabilitation, for cancer control and the like. None of these grants has anything whatsoever to do with health insurance except in so far as providing a foundation stone for the successful operation of a system of health insurance.
What allocations are to take place? Are we to conclude that because the government is proposing, under certain conditions, inconsistent with the promises that it made during

Supply-Health and Welfare the election, to include tuberculosis and mental illness, they are going, by allocations of the funds provided for in these two particular categories, to spend less money for tuberculosis control. The moneys spent for mental illness have nothing to do with hospital insurance at all. The moneys in these two particular categories had to do with another phase altogether.
Remember what I am discussing now is a project of health insurance, a project designed not to assist the provinces in respect of obligations that they have assumed but to assist individuals in Canada in meeting their hospital costs. The money spent under the tuberculosis control grant and under the mental health grant are moneys spent for the purpose of providing facilities. They are not moneys provided to help individuals meet their hospital costs; they are designed to provide research in these various fields, to give the provinces the wherewithal to employ the necessary personnel and to carry out the general objects and purposes of these particular grants. Therefore, I hope the minister will give very careful consideration to the reply he gave a few days ago and to the observation he made a moment ago.
Take the hospital construction grant. That has nothing to do directly with hospital insurance. That grant was designed to place the provinces and the communities of our country in a position where, when we had hospital insurance in being, there would be the necessary hospital facilities available to make that scheme practicable and possible of operation. Under that grant, with the assistance of the provinces and with the major assistance of communities and voluntary bodies, we would be able together to provide for the construction of somewhere between 70,000 and 75,000 additional hospital beds.
That was a very essential foundation for the operation of a system of hospital insurance. Those grants will have to be continued because the country is growing. The need for hospital beds will continue and if there is to be any allocation of those grants and the moneys used for this particular purpose are to be transferred to take care of part of the federal share of hospital insurance we shall be going back on the commitment which the previous administration made to the provincial governments. That has had the greatest possible consequences. Therefore, I hope the minister will give careful consideration to maintaining the grants in the form in which they are. Of course he will be confronted, as time goes on, with the necessity, possibly, of increasing them if we are to maintain the pace which I believe the provincial, the municipal and the federal


governments have been able to achieve in Canada during the past decade or so.
I would remind the minister that he told us quite frankly the other day when I asked him a question that the amendments contemplated to the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act had to do with the provision of payment so that one province which was prepared to embark upon a scheme would not find itself handicapped as a result of the fact that at the present time there are no agreements with any one of the six provinces, a situation which I believe would have been avoided if the kind of care and interest had been pursued which I suggested, and about the lack of which I complained.
If that is the only amendment the government has in mind I am forced under these circumstances to point out at this time that it represents but a small portion of the commitments, or of the position which was taken by hon. gentlemen, now on the treasury benches, when they were in opposition. When they were in opposition they said that the hospital insurance measure which the government of that day introduced was a good one but it did not go far enough, notwithstanding the fact that the federal government of that day committed itself to an expenditure of at least $200 million in the first year of complete operation, a sum that represented half of the total cost of hospital insurance in Canada.
They said that we should go farther; that we should do something about taking care of a share in depreciation costs. What is the government going to do about that? They made strong arguments on this side that our measure was weak because it did not include a decision on the part of the federal government to share in the costs of depreciation. Does the government now take the position that it was wrong in urging these things when sitting on this side of the house?
What about the costs of administration? When we introduced hospital insurance we were told that it was inadequate because it was unfair to impose upon the provinces the responsibility for the full cost of administration. We pointed out at that time that the provinces were not going to be called upon to find as much new money as the federal government was going to have to find and that the provinces could be well left with the responsibility of providing for assistance in the matter of depreciation and in the matter of administration if that were thought the desirable thing to do.
But our reply in that particular was not accepted by hon. gentlemen opposite and they now have the responsibility of discharging the obligations which they sought

to impose on the previous government or of admitting now that the arguments they made on that occasion were not valid or sound. We have the right to ask the Minister of National Health and Welfare what he proposes to do about these particular claims that were made by the opposition of the government of the day, claims that have a great interest and importance in the minds of the various hospital administrations and the various voluntary bodies all over the country who, I know, are most vitally interested in the position taken by hon. gentlemen opposite with regard to the questions of depreciation and the cost of administration.
Therefore I ask the government to realize the importance of this matter. It is not too late for the minister to rise now in his place and to explain why agreements have not been concluded and to give us assurance and evidence that the delay that has taken place will be corrected by a new effort on the part of the government to carry out its obligations in respect of the act-

Mr. Chairman, I should like at the outset to join with the hon. member for Essex East in paying tribute to the staff and officials of the Department of National Health and Welfare. Obviously some of us have not had 96698-173
Supply-Health and Welfare the advantage of the contacts with the officers and staff that the hon. member for Essex East enjoyed for a number of years, but we have met them in committee, we have dealings with them from time to time when we have cases to pursue, and we also have the advantage of the excellent material that the research workers in the department prepare.
I should like also to express appreciation of the tremendous importance of this department to the life of the people of Canada, and I congratulate the minister for having been called upon to preside over the affairs of such an important department. However, I must also join with the hon. member for Essex East in expressing the regret of this party at the delay of the present government in implementing the provisions of the the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act. Everyone knows that it is the view of the C.C.F. that we should have on our statute books much more advanced legislation than that act. We feel the time has come for an over-all national insurance plan with provision for provincial administration but with provision for coverage of all aspects of illness on the part of our people.
Nevertheless, we do appreciate the step along the way taken in 1948 by the inauguration of the health grants program and the further step taken in the spring of this year through the enactment of the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act. Because we appreciate these steps as being in the right direction, we regret very much that the implementation of the act seems to be so slow in coming under the aegis of the present government.
While the former minister was speaking I heard the minister interject that there had been no delay, but I submit that there is evidence of nothing else. It is not my intention to repeat the speech I made in the House of Commons on November 18 when on behalf of our party I moved an amendment to the motion to go into supply. But I would remind the minister that it was pointed out then that the present session was opened on an historic occasion with the speech from the throne read by Her Majesty the Queen but that in that speech there was no mention of health insurance or hospital insurance in any way. I remind the minister that to the first number of questions we on this side of the house asked with respect to whether anything was going to be done about hospital insurance or whether the matter was even on the agenda for the then forthcoming federal-provincial conference the answers were in the negative or evasive.

Supply-Health and Welfare
For several weeks it looked as though nothing was happening. Then tor a period ot a couple of weeks the air vibrated with assurances and promises. Strangely enough, those two weeks followed the moving from this corner of a non-confidence motion on the question of implementing the hospital insurance plan. The Minister of National Health and Welfare, from whom we had had difficulty in getting any answers to questions, got into that debate and assured us that the matter was being studied in his department. The Prime Minister previously had been unable to assure us that the matter would be discussed at the federal-provincial conference but he got into that debate when the confidence of the house in the government was under discussion and assured us that all matters in relation to the hospital insurance legislation would be discussed at the federal-provincial conference if the provincial representatives wished to discuss those matters.
Then the conference itself was held and at that conference there were discussions regarding the implementation of the hospital insurance plan. We were led to believe that those discussions centred in the main around two points, one being the removal of the six-province requirement and the other the inclusion of mental and tuberculosis institutions within the four corners of this legislation. A few days after that we had statements in the house-both on the initiative of the Prime Minister and in reply to questions-to the effect that the implementation of this legislation would be proceeded with; in fact, that we would get it sooner under the Tories than we would have had it under the Liberals.
These vibrant, sonorous assurances rang through the chamber for a few days and as a result we were led to believe that something would be done. Hence the pace of our questions slackened. But what has happened? Any evidence that anything is being done has died down completely. In fact, although the Prime Minister has been pleased to add to the list of items to be dealt with in this session of parliament, he still has not given the house notice, nor has his colleague the Minister of National Health and Welfare, of any legislation to amend the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act. In answer to questions the Minister of National Health and Welfare has admitted that if there are to be any amendments to that act they will relate only to the removal of the six province requirement.
With regard to the other matter, namely mental and tuberculosis hospitals, the minister now says that this is a matter of government policy and that any announcement

of any decision made with regard to that question will be made in due course. That latest word, in fact, was given by the Minister of National Health and Welfare as recently as December 17, in response to questions of mine on the orders of the day as recorded in Hansard at page 2473 and 2474 of that date.
In other words, Mr. Chairman, it all adds up to one big zero. No agreements have been signed. No action has been taken. No legislation has been placed on the order paper. In fact, it seems to us that there is on the part of the new administration no appreciation of the importance, social significance and urgency of this legislation to make a beginning in the field of health insurance by doing something with regard to hospital insurance.
The minister may not like my saying that it adds up to nothing, but I submit that that is a fair statement of the case. As I reminded the Conservatives when we debated this matter on November 18 and 19, they were loud and strong last spring in their insistence that the act should be improved; and the point on which they were loudest and strongest was that mental and tubercular hospitals should be included. Indeed, it was they who moved an amendment or two to that effect, even as late in the game as on third reading of the bill, when they moved an amendment to refer the bill back to a committee for the purpose of reconsidering that aspect of the matter.
I remind them that during the election campaign-and I have here excerpts from some of the items that appeared in the press -the Prime Minister made certain promises. According to the Minister of Finance we must not quote what the Conservatives said in the election campaign unless the Prime Minister said it. But during the election campaign the Prime Minister, amongst other items, promised that the Conservatives, if elected, would bring mental and tubercular hospitals under the provisions of this act. Yet, Mr. Chairman, nothing has been done on this matter for which the Conservatives were so strong last spring. The Minister of National Health and Welfare, by his answer on December 17 to which I have made reference, made it clear that that idea has just about been scuttled so far as this present government is concerned. If he wants to say that we have been assured that we are still going to get the amendment to the act to remove the six-province provision, I ask him what value there is in that now. If he replies to me that we moved an amendment to that effect last spring, I remind him that we moved that amendment at a time when only

five provinces had signified their willingness to come into the plan. But shortly after that, a sixth province indicated its willingness to participate. Now that there are six agreeing provinces, I say that the six-province provision no longer has any practical limitation so far as the implementation of this act is concerned.
So what the government proposes to do is this. All that has come out of these assurances, all that has come out of the supposed study and attention that has been given to the matter, and the supposed interest that the new government has in this legislation, is the promise that somewhere along in the piece we are going to get an amendment that does not mean anything at all. We are going to get the removal of the six-province requirement at a time when six provinces have already agreed. That being the case, Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that we have to do to this government exactly what we had to do to the former government, we have to keep on poking and prodding, trying to get them to take action.
