It would be out of order, Mr. Chairman, if I were to rehash the debates that took place on the amending bill that was before the house some weeks ago. At this moment, however, it is the law of the land that the old age security pension, among others, is $55 per month. It is perfectly in order for the government to bring in another bill at this session raising it to a higher amount just as it is perfectly in order for a member in this session to urge that the law, as it now stands, should be changed to bring greater benefit to our people.
However, what I propose to do is to suggest that this whole subject does need further and very serious study. Here again I might point out that on one of those occasions when we had before the house a motion of non-confidence in the government we got something out of it. These motions of non-confidence are apparently not without value. It is only when you have a motion of non-confidence or by prodding and poking that you seem to get something out of the government across the way.
During the debate on one of these motions we got a promise from the Prime Minister that the government would study the system of old age and survivors' insurance in the United States and other similar systems to see if some way could not be found to improve our old age pension situation in Canada. We have heard nothing about it since and that is exactly our fear, that this sort of thing gets promised in the heat of debate; this sort of thing gets promised to get the government off the hook, but then time has a way of going on with this government as it did with the former government.
The fact is that we need to raise our sights a great deal so far as old age security is concerned. I can make these remarks brief because I said something along this line in another debate a few days ago. There was a time when it took an heroic effort on the part of my predecessor, Mr. J. S. Woods-worth, to sell to parliament the idea of an old age pension at all, even with a means test and even at a rate of only $20 per month. But in due course it got acceptance, although it was not until the first old age pension bill had been defeated over in the other place. Then it took us a number of years to sell the idea that there should be a pension for our senior citizens, as a matter of right, without a means test. I can remember in my time here the occasions when we were told this simply could not be done. We
Supply-Health and Welfare got that principle established, that a pension is a social responsibility and that a pension should be as of right without a means test.
Mr. Chairman, we think we ought to go further, and get to the place where we recognize that people having made their contributions to the economy and life of the country should in their retirement years have a pension, not just sufficient to exist on but sufficient to retire on in dignity and decency; and that means a pension much higher than $55 a month, much higher, even, than the $75 we advocated in the last election campaign.
That means, Mr. Chairman, we may have to do some more thinking about this problem; we may have to go in for a plan that has two aspects; we may have to go in for a combination of the present universal pension on a flat rate basis and a contributory pension based on income supplementary to the flat rate pension. We may have to find a way to provide for portable pensions in industry; a way of making it possible for people to move from one job to another and maintain their pension rights. We may have to recast our income tax structure in relation to old age pensions.
I had something to say about this matter in the special committee on estimates on Thursday, April 12, 1956, as reported at page 284 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence of that committee. I suggested then that some of us who had lived through the means test era would never agree to the re-imposition of a means test, and I am sure the hon. member for Essex East now agrees with me, even if he did not always agree with me on it, that to talk about pensions related to need is to talk about the re-imposition of the means test with all the hurt and misery it imposed on so many of our people.
At the same time it is possible by means of a steeply graded income tax and by a special income tax on pensions received by people who have higher incomes to even out the effect of higher pensions. What I am suggesting is, with all these things, the possibility of raising tremendously the present $55 pension, and taking care of the wealthy person by a change in the income tax, by introducing legislation to provide for portable pensions in industry, by introducing a national industrial pension plan as proposed by the Canadian Labour Congress, or a national pension on a contributory basis supplementary to our old age pension on a universal basis. It is possible, if we do these things on the bases I have suggested, to achieve a raising of our sights.
We had the Gordon commission report about a year ago. We do not hear much about it these days, but I remind hon. members

Supply-Health and Welfare that the Gordon commission forecast a substantial increase in the gross national product 20 or 25 years hence. The commission forecast an increase in salaries and wages and we have got to meet the kind of increase forecast by the Gordon commission with the recognition that we may have to find a way whereby all our people on reaching retirement age will enjoy pensions, not just at the charitable level but sufficient to enable them to enjoy decency and dignity in retirement.
I see you moving to the edge of your chair, Mr. Chairman, so may I conclude these remarks-to come back later, because we are in committee of supply-by calling to the attention of the Minister of National Health and Welfare an excellent document entitled "Age and Opportunity" prepared by the welfare council of greater Winnipeg, which is a study of the experience of older citizens in the greater Winnipeg area. This report indicates that to a surprising extent our older people have as their main source of income their old age pensions, which means we have to get that amount up a lot higher. I draw attention also to the fact that this very responsible body urges very strongly on page 41 of this report that there should now be a complete review of the whole question of old age security provisions similar to that undertaken by a joint committee of the Senate and of the House of Commons back in 1950. All of us who were members of that committee and had the assistance of the staff of the minister's department believed it was one of the finest committees which ever met in parliament. It did a good job and it made recommendations on the basis of which effective steps were taken. We think it is time for another such committee to meet and study these matters with a view to revamping our pension system so as to maintain our older citizens, not just at a subsistence level but at a level which would enable them in retirement to participate in the higher standard of life now possible in this country.

subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words on the first item that is before us at the present time. Like the two previous speakers, I also should like to pay my tribute to the officials of the Department of National Health and Welfare. During the last parliament it was my privilege to head the committee on health and welfare within our little group, and I had occasion more than once to visit the various heads of departments within the Department of National Health and Welfare and I always got a very cordial response. I was given all the information that was available-it was far too much

for me to assimilate-and I appreciate their efforts very much to be helpful and agreeable.
Like the other two speakers, I also was keenly disappointed in the action or lack of action on the part of this government in implementing hospital insurance. We listened to the debates in the last parliament, and have listened to the promises made throughout the country that this would be implemented speedily; that mental and tubercular care would be included and that various changes would be made in the act, which would be a much better and much more suitable act; and that greater financial assistance should be given to the provinces.
However, a strange curtain of secrecy seems to have been woven around this question of hospital insurance since parliament assembled here in October, and it is not just with regard to the department of health. We can ask questions of practically every department in the government, and we are given the brush-off in most cases. In this respect our questions as to what progress is being made, how other provinces are reacting to the plan and whether arrangements to cover mental and tubercular care are being considered, have been particularly unsuccessful in obtaining any definite information. We are told that all is proceeding well; we are asked to have confidence in the government.
Mr. Chairman, we may have confidence in the government, but our confidence may be growing less day by day due to the fact that there is no co-operation between the government and members of the house to give us information about what is going on. I say with all seriousness that there cannot be co-operation unless we are advised of what this government is doing; we must at least have some knowledge that they have at heart these problems with which we are concerned. We should be told just a little bit of what is being done in order to sustain our confidence.
I am now going to make a few general remarks and when the detailed items are before us I will perhaps deal with them more specifically. The Department of National Health and Welfare is the second largest in terms of expenditure of all the departments of government, second only to the Department of National Defence, but in many ways it is of the greatest importance to the people of Canada of all departments of government. It is greater in importance than the Department of National Defence which spends more money because the greatest asset of any nation is the health of its people. At the moment I am more concerned with the subject of health than with the subject of welfare and so I will confine my remarks to that

aspect of the department. It is the duty of our department of health to ensure that we have a nation of healthy and vigorous people and so it must be constantly on the alert to guard, promote and maintain the health of Canadians.
Today the emphasis in the field of health is on prevention. The medical profession and all our health organizations are today gearing their efforts towards the prevention of sickness and disease rather than cure. In order to facilitate that program of prevention, in other words to combat disease before it occurs, we must have an additional speeded up program of research and study.
The battle that will be waged by our research men against sickness and disease will require a greatly enlarged staff and we will have to provide additional training facilities in order to prepare technicians and experts to carry on this research. This will also require the expenditure of vast sums of money but I am satisfied that the people of Canada will not begrudge money for this important aspect of promoting their own health and welfare and in building a nation of which each of us may well be proud. That is a general review, as I see it, of the need for expanding and continuing research into the prevention of sickness and disease.
One aspect of illness with which I wish to deal in greater detail at the present time is mental illness. This is the No. 1 health problem not only in Canada but throughout the world. It is difficult today to pick up a magazine or newspaper of any repute without finding a report of advances that are being made in the study of mental disorders and in devising cures for the various phases of mental illness with which our people are beset. I sometimes wonder if we are completely on the right track in this respect. Many patients who visit doctors at the present time complaining of stomach disorders, skin disorders, neuritis, sciatica and migraine headaches invariably have their disorder diagnosed as being attributable to nerves. If a person with a chronic skin disorder visits a doctor there is a strong likelihood that the doctor's verdict will be that the patient suffers from nervous eczema. A person suffering from what used to be called gastric stomach disorder or some other common stomach ailment is today invariably told that he has a nervous stomach. Those suffering from various neuralgic pains, sciatica, neuritis or migraine headaches are advised they are suffering from just plain "nerves". The treatment for those conditions, of course, is frequently psychiatry or sedation. I think that in too many cases our doctors today do not have the time to devote to treating these
Supply-Health and Welfare cases which seem to be increasing in number and an easy way out is to prescribe sedation. This of course has a temporary effect and may bring relief but I have often wondered if it is the proper relief.
I was recently intrigued by a series of articles which recently appeared in a publication written by two noted doctors, one from Montreal and one from the province of Saskatchewan. I will not mention any names but I will say that these men are approaching the problem of mental illness in a fresh way. In cases of chronic skin disease they are attempting to find if there is some physical cause for the disease. They are of the view that perhaps chronic skin diseases which can be extremely irritating are the cause of the nervous condition in the patient instead of the nervous temperament of the person being the cause of the skin disease. In other words we are coming back to the question: which came first the chicken or the egg? That is the problem these and other doctors are trying to determine today in the field of mental health. I suspect that all too often doctors have said that the patient's condition was caused by nerves whereas the nervous condition has in fact been the result of physical disability.
The chief of the mental health department of the province of Saskatchewan and the doctor in charge of the research institution there are taking that attitude. They are obtaining wonderful results by treating people who for years have been considered incurable mental patients. They are attacking the problem from the physical standpoint and have discovered that in many cases a physical disability has been the cause of a nervous condition from which patients have been condemned to suffer for many years. Many people have been cured and are leaving that institution to which they were condemned, if you will, and in which they expected to spend the rest of their lives. The problem of mental illness will require a vast amount of study, research and the expenditure of large sums of money.
Hon. members of this house frequently ask the government to cut down expenditures and yet we always seem to be hollering for it to spend more money. I would suggest, however, that there be absolutely no cutback in grants to provinces, universities and health organizations of any kind that are furthering the cause of research into any of the sicknesses and illnesses that plague our people at the present time. I would make a special plea that the grant for research and study in the field of mental illness be greatly increased

Supply-Health and Welfare because it is one of our greatest problems today and it looks as though it will be a continuing problem of increasing proportions unless some drastic action is taken.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, as I said we shall go into the minor details of the huge expenditure contained in these estimates. We shall study the estimates as we go along, but I should like to emphasize this. I hope the Department of National Health and Welfare will do absolutely nothing, in the way of curtailing expenses, to interfere with grants to the provinces, to universities and to health organizations in any plans they may have that bring promise of winning the battle in the prevention of disease and sickness among our people.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have been privileged to serve as parliamentary assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare since last August. In the brief space of less than five months I have been greatly impressed with the wide range of the department's activities connected with health and welfare, and with the way in which the work of this department reaches out to touch almost literally the lives and the way of life of almost every one of the 17 million people living in Canada.
In terms of personnel employed in this department, it is not one of the larger ones in the government of Canada. In terms of personnel employed, the establishment this year for the entire department numbers fewer than 5,000, which is only about three per cent of the public service taken as a whole. It does not compare in size, Mr. Chairman, therefore, with the giant establishments of national defence, post office, veterans affairs, transport or the finance department. The entire department actually employs only about half as many people as the national employment service and the unemployment insurance commission.
On the score of budget and expenditures, however, this department is one of the largest and most important of all departments in the public service, with a budget that will this year run somewhere close to $1 billion. This is true when supplementary estimates and additional expenditures arising out of recent legislative changes are added to the $918 million published in the blue book of estimates at the beginning of the current year. Only national defence, with a budget of almost $lf billion, and finance with a budget of $1,150 million, exceed the total size of the annual budget of expenditure of the Department of National Health and Welfare for the current year.
Perhaps the most outstanding feature of this budget of close to $1 billion is that only

$75 million requires to be voted by parliament. The balance of the $925 million consists of statutory items, where the authority for the expenditure is written into the legislation itself. It continues from year to year as long as the legislation remains on the statute books and consequently an annual appropriation is not required to be voted by this house.
I should like to repeat these two figures, Mr. Chairman, because I doubt whether many members realize how large a proportion of the expenditures of this department is dependent upon the annual procedure of voting the estimates in this house. The sum of $925 million, or roughly 92.5 per cent of all the funds required by the Department of National Health and Welfare this year, is provided automatically by the statutory authority contained in the legislation which this department administers. Only $75 million, or 7.5 per cent of total expenditures, requires to be specifically voted by this parliament.
What I have just said with reference to the small percentage of this department's estimates requiring a vote of parliament does not in any way lessen the importance of close and detailed scrutiny by the members of this house when the estimates come up for consideration. In offering our comments and criticisms with respect to the estimates of this and other departments we are discharging our responsibilities as elected representatives of the people, sent here to ensure the wise and proper administration of the funds which are taken from the people by way of taxes and provided to the various departments to enable them to carry on the administration of the public services of the country.
Since this is the first occasion when this new parliament has had an opportunity to consider the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare, and since there are so many newly elected members of this present parliament, one might have thought that the work of the department and the programs which it administers would require a good deal of explanation and elaboration at this time. However, the fact is that while the estimates in the formal sense come before this parliament now for the first time for detailed discussion, most of the programs administered by the department have already received a good deal of the attention of this house in the weeks that have elapsed since we first met here on October 14. In fact, the second thing that impresses me as I examine the estimates of this department is this: already, within the short space of two months, the new Conservative administration, under the leadership of our present Prime Minister, has

introduced and obtained the passage of amendments effecting major improvements in social legislation now on the statute books of this country. It took almost 20 years for the previous Liberal administration to place on the statute books such enactments as the Unemployment Insurance Act, the Old Age Security Act, the Old Age Assistance Act, the Blind Persons Act, the Disabled Persons Act and the Unemployment Assistance Act.

We will forget that just now. I must tell you something. You have been up in this house about 30 times. This is my first time up. Will you lay off, or I will have to interrupt you some day.
It took only two months, Mr. Chairman, for this government to effect important and far-reaching changes in all of this legislation. We have amended the Old Age Security Act to raise the amount of benefit from $46 to $55 a month and to reduce the residence requirement from 20 to 10 years. We have made similar changes in the Old Age Assistance Act, in the Disabled Persons Act and in the assistance given to the blind people. These changes have brought great comfort and satisfaction into the lives of over 900,000 aging and handicapped men and women in all parts of Canada. Through the Unemployment Assistance Act, passed only this week, we have offered a much larger measure of financial assistance to the provinces which will have the effect of improving the standards of relief and services to needy persons in many parts of Canada, because it will place the provinces, and particularly the municipalities of this country, in a much better position than before to deal generously with the needs of these unfortunate people.
Here we have no fewer than five pieces of legislation, Mr. Chairman, all of them administrated under the direction of the Minister of National Health and Welfare, touching directly the lives of over one million people in this country; I think it is to the very great credit of this administration that in the short space of two months with all the difficulties involved in taking over the reins of government after 22 years in opposition the first priority on the time and attention of this new parliament has been the amelioration of the lot of our senior citizens, our aged blind and disabled and needy persons. This is a very striking demonstration, Mr. Chairman, that the present administration is close to the people, responsive to their needs and gives first 96698-174
Supply-Health and Welfare priority as a good government should to the human and social needs of the people to whom it is responsible.
The five pieces of legislation to which I have referred are not, of course, the only ones on which the government has taken action or with respect to which it has announced its intention of taking action in the very short space of time since it took over the reins of office. The house has already debated and approved a very important measure for the extension of seasonal benefits in connection with unemployment insurance, a social measure which lies outside the scope of the Department of National Health and Welfare but which none the less is an important item in the list of accomplishments in the social welfare field during the present session of parliament.
Another important announcement concerning changes in the six-provinces requirement in the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act has also been made by the Prime Minister during the course of the current session. Since this is the last day on which the house will be sitting during the calendar year 1957, I think I am safe in assuming that this important change in the hospital insurance legislation will not be brought down until some time early in 1958. Its introduction and passage will furnish still one more example of the rapid forward strides that have been made in the field of health and social legislation under the new administration.
I should like to say as one member of the house, Mr. Chairman, that on the basis of the record I have outlined I think the new government is to be heartily commended for the creditable record it has achieved, particularly in the health and social welfare fields, and for the almost unbelievable speed with which it has acted in these matters. To record our satisfaction with these accomplishments is not, however, to suggest that our work is finished. As we examine in detail the work of the Department of National Health and Welfare, we will no doubt find other areas, both in the administrative and legislative fields, for changes and improvements.
One of the most important and valuable programs undertaken on the health side of the department is that represented by the national health grants. Through this program more than $35 million is made available in support of the health services and facilities of the provinces of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words before the item carries. If I understood the minister correctly, when we began the discussion of the estimates of the department he indicated that he was going to follow the bad example of his predecessor and was not going to give us an outline of the activities of the department or of his plans for the future. While there may have been some reasonable excuse for the former minister not having done so in recent years on the ground that over a period of years he had made a good many statements and that as he had no new plans to offer it would simply be repetitious if he were to do so, nevertheless it came as a bit of a surprise to me that, with the bold, new government to which the minister belongs, according to statements he and others on the treasury benches have made, he did not see fit to give us some indication of just how the new broom was going to sweep clean. Perhaps after listening to the suggestions and comments made by members like the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre the minister may see fit to give us some indication before his estimates are carried as to just how we are going to see the new broom in action.
I noticed that the parliamentary assistant gave us quite a resume of the legislation that had been put on the statute books by the former administration over a period of 22 years. He said what all of us in the house know, that certain amendments have been made to some of these acts since this session began. However, when some of us have the opportunity of assessing just how these amendments are working out perhaps we can be excused for not being quite as enthusiastic with regard to them as was the hon. member for London.
I have no desire to enter into an extended discussion of the subject. However, I should like to make it quite clear, along with other members from the province of British Columbia, that the delay and the silence with respect to when national hospital insurance is going to become effective in our province,

referred to by some other speakers, are something about which we are concerned.
According to some reports I have seen in the British Columbia press we have the prospect that our provincial administration may be going to carry out some retrenchment of expenditures in this coming year. It is reported that one of the reasons for that retrenchment is some decline in the revenues that come from our provincial sales tax from which, as the minister knows, the expenses of our hospital insurance services are defrayed. If that is the case, then of course the minister will appreciate the fact that some of us at least in British Columbia are going to have a greater concern as to the future progress of our hospital system in British Columbia than perhaps we have had even before this time.
Any of us who have had any opportunity of a connection with any local hospital board in the province of British Columbia know that our local hospital boards in that province have been labouring under very serious difficulties in maintaining adequate services because of the financial limitations that are being imposed upon them by the provincial administration. For that reason we are more than ever concerned that the financial assistance that is provided under the act that we passed in this house should become available in our province at the earliest possible date.
I am not going to say any more on that subject except that I know the suggestion just made by the hon. member for York South is one which those of us in British Columbia who have seen the problems of our hospital boards there would most heartily second. On more than one occasion in previous discussions we have made it clear that because of the drastic increases in hospital construction costs that have taken place since the present figure was set we feel it to be unrealistic in that it does not bear anything like the same relationship to the costs of providing hospital beds and hospital accommodation that it did originally.
References have already been made to the fact that earlier this year we in this house passed a further increase to the old age pension. However, in our consideration of the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare, and in our assessment of the effectiveness of the activities that are carried on under the responsibility of this minister, I think we must consider such things as this particular old age pension increase in the context of the general situation in the country. While on the face of it an extra $9 a month appears 96698-174J
Supply-Health and Welfare to be a very welcome addition to the income of those who are dependent primarily on that basic old age security pension,-and the same would apply to some of the other pensions that were increased-nevertheless I think part of our responsibility as members of parliament is to remain alert to what is happening to that money after it goes into the hands of the old age pensioners. Now surely we will have to determine where the responsibility for health lies and also where we are going to get the money to pay for it. If the provinces are to be responsible for public health and they do not have the fields of taxation necessary to take care of it, then they will have to come to the federal government. Of course I will agree that the federal government should be prepared to meet some of those costs, but on the other hand if they are going to insist that the details of administration in so far as items being included or excluded are concerned being a federal responsibility, then I suggest they are very definitely intruding on provincial jurisdiction.
There are perhaps some provinces who feel that their resources are just not sufficient to meet the conditions in Bill 320. If that is the case I think this department or this government should take another look and try to come up with something which will be acceptable to more of the provinces. Some of the richer provinces can probably meet these conditions and there are certain items, I understand, which are not contained in Bill No. 320 but which are already being looked after by certain provincial governments. It seems to me on the basis of what I have heard-and I am now asking the minister for clarification-that the provinces are not too satisfied with this bill and I would like to know specifically what objections have been raised.

I have two very brief questions which I think had best be asked on this item because I have not found any other items in the estimates to which they seem related. In my riding we have three travelling clinics. They are very small boats of about 50 feet in length with a crew of two in which a doctor travels around the territory allocated to him and visits the various settlements in his district on a regular schedule. Now these travelling clinics were provided by grants from the Department of National Health and Welfare. There is a need on these boats at the present time for the provision of radio telephones. These boats, as I said, have a
Supply-Health and Welfare crew of only two. Sometimes they have to carry a nurse, and at other times they have to take a patient to hospital, and they are powered by only a single engine. We have had one or two narrow escapes due to the engine giving out, and it was only by a miracle that the people on board saved their lives. This could have been avoided had the ships been equipped with a radio telephone service which would have enabled them to contact other ships lying in the harbours nearby. On one particular occasion a doctor and a nurse had to row several miles in a small boat in very rough seas before they could get aid. I have made some inquiries about this matter, and I understand the initiative in this respect must come from the provinces, and my first question to the minister is whether any representations have been made to his department by the provincial government of Newfoundland to have this equipment provided.
My second question has to do with a certificate necessary for boats sailing to foreign ports. I believe it is called a deratization certificate. That means it is a certificate which certifies that the ship is free from rodents, and ships without this certificate are not allowed to enter certain foreign ports. Prior to confederation the provincial authority provided this certificate at St. John's but when confederation took place the province was no longer able to supply it and our ships had to go to Halifax in order to get this certificate to enable them to sail to foreign ports. Sailing all the way from St. John's Newfoundland to Halifax just to get a certificate caused tremendous inconvenience as well as extra expense, as hon. members will realize. The matter was brought to the attention of the former government and steps were being taken to have the situation remedied. My second question to the minister is as to whether these steps have been finalized or, if not, what stage of progress has now been reached.

speechtext:
Listening to the parliamentary assistant speak I wondered whether he had gone through Hansard for the last few years looking up some of the speeches by the former minister of health and welfare, because the remarks he made had a very familiar ring. They had been brought up to date a little but nevertheless they consisted of extolling the government for the amount of money it was spending on this department, just as the former minister would have done.
I suggest, as my colleague the hon. member for Comox-Alberni has done, that there have been no changes in policy as a result of the so-called change of government resulting

Supply-Health and Welfare from the election on June 10 last. We had hoped that with the replacement of the old government there might be some fresh approach to the question of health and welfare in Canada, but I notice that the estimates we are considering today remain unchanged; to the best of by knowledge I do not think there has been a single alteration in any one of the estimates drawn up by the minister of health in the former government.
I am particularly interested in the fate of the hospital plan. We have had provincial hospitalization in my own province for quite a number of years, and we are very proud of that plan-the first to be instituted by any government on the North American continent. We did not wait a long time after we took office, but we set out immediately to bring in the hospitalization plan at the earliest possible moment. That was done, and any pride which we have expressed, any boasting in which we might have been inclined to indulge, was done after the plan had been put into effect and after the people of the province had been enjoying its benefits. So I would suggest there is a great deal to be done by the present minister of health before he and his colleagues in the house can, for obvious political purposes, boast about what the present government is doing.
We are quite concerned about the question of tubercular sanatoria and mental hospitals, and we hope the government does not intend to proceed with the policy of giving with one hand and taking away with the other hand, and that any sums paid with respect to the hospital plan will in no way affect the general picture in so far as dominion-provincial fiscal relationships are concerned.
The hon. member for York South raised a point which I had long felt had been overlooked and ignored by the previous government, and apparently the present government is also turning a deaf ear to entreaties made in respect of it. I know the present regulations provide for a grant for capital construction of an active treatment bed of $1,000 per bed, and this grant is to be matched or .exceeded by the provincial government, and in no circumstances shall the federal grant exceed one-third of the total over-all cost of capital construction. I ask the minister, since this proportion of one-third is involved, why he does not consider it advisable, and indeed necessary, to make a grant of one-third of the total over-all cost of a hospital bed? As the hon. member for York South pointed out, $1,000 per bed is a far cry from the type of assistance which the federal government ought to be granting. I have not with me at the moment the figures for the cost of construction per hospital bed in different parts

of the country, but I know there are areas in Canada where it costs about $13,000 or $14,000 per bed.
In the circumstances a grant of one-third, which the regulations mention as being the maximum permissible amount which the federal government can provide, in other words a payment of some $4,000 a bed, would not be out of line, and I agree with one of the hon. minister's colleagues on his own side of the house who stated that it is nonsense to think the federal government is making any worth while contribution to hospital construction as long as it is limiting the grant per bed to a mere $1,000.
Hospital construction costs continue to rise. The former minister of health was quite prepared to turn a deaf ear to the entreaties we made over the years respecting this item, but I had hoped that the new minister would see fit to bring in increases with regard to this very important item of construction. The arguments which have frequently been made against a hospital plan for Canada are that there are not enough hospital beds to go around. We heard the same in Saskatchewan; the Liberal party in that province opposed the plan, and the most frequently used argument for doing so was that there were not enough hospital beds available to make it possible. If there are not enough beds, the obvious answer lies in hospital construction. If there are not enough beds in the provinces or in Canada we have to build them. That is the obvious answer and I presume the federal grant was designed to encourage hospital construction in Canada as the parliamentary assistant pointed out. Surely the minister is not going to suggest to hon. members of this committee that $1,000 out of a capital construction cost anywhere from 12 to 14 times that amount is a grant of a sufficient size to actively encourage hospital construction in Canada. I would hope that the minister would give serious consideration to the future program of activities to be carried on by his department.
I note that there has not been too much enthusiasm on the part of the government so a far as a national hospital plan is concerned and I think that is completely understandable. There has been a Conservative government in Ontario for a great number of years now and in spite of that fact there is no hospitalization plan in that province. I suggest that the reason the premier of Ontario decided to have his province become one of the six provinces to ask for inclusion in the national hospital plan was more out of a desire to put the former government on the spot than it was to actively promote the establishment of a hospitalization plan

throughout this country. As long as the provinces of Quebec and Ontario would refuse to participate it gave the former minister of national health and welfare what he considered an excellent excuse for going up and down the country pointing out that the Liberal government wanted to bring in a hospital plan but was being thwarted in so doing by the two major provinces, Ontario and Quebec.

I realize that. I have read editorial opinions in newspapers in the province of Ontario by opponents of the hospital plan who argued that you cannot have a hospital plan because there are not enough hospital beds but I remind hon. gentlemen that that sort of reasoning did not prevail in my own province. We wanted to see a hospital plan in effect and so we proceeded to put one in effect. We did not talk about it or attempt to find excuses for not doing so. There is no reason why the province of Ontario, one of the wealthier provinces of Canada, could not have given the people who live in that province a hospital plan many years ago. When Premier Frost put the former government on the spot by saying, "Yes, we are prepared to go ahead," I am sure it caused the former minister of national health and welfare a great deal of acute embarrassment. Mr. Frost's attitude is illustrated by the fact that he put certain limitations on his acceptance. He did not want to bring it in right away and suggested it be done in 1959.
When the government changed I hoped that the new administration would accept the fact that there are two provinces in Canada which have had successful hospital plans in operation for a number of years and which have been urging year in and year out that the federal government fulfil its pledge by bringing in a national health insurance plan. In my own province we look upon our hospitalization plan as being the effort which the province is putting forward in order to encourage the development of a general health plan for all of Canada. We had hoped that when the federal government brought in a comprehensive national health plan we would be able to supply the people in our province
Supply-Health and Welfare with full medical health care, hospitalization, doctor care and the type of treatment all the people of Canada have a right to expect and enjoy but we have witnessed procrastination and stalling on the part of the present government. When we asked the minister whether the provinces of Saskatchewan and British Columbia which have plans in operation would be offered agreements and whether this government would make it possible for those provinces to enter the national scheme on January 1 next we received nothing but evasive answers. I suggest there is no good reason whatever why those two provinces should not be able to enjoy any benefit which might accrue from the hospital plan brought in by the former government and which, since the present government is simply continuing the policies adopted by the former administration, we presume the present government will carry through.
We in the C.C.F. look upon a hospital plan as being merely a part of a general over-all health plan to provide the Canadian people with the type of medical and health care necessary in this day and age. We Canadians boast about our wealth, our gross national product, about the number of automobiles we have and the material wealth that abounds in this country but I suggest that the real yardstick by which to measure a nation's wealth is the manner in which its federal government provides for the social welfare and health needs of the people of that country. It is not the number of people who drive big cars or the number who live in expensive homes that is important. The government must be judged on the basis of the provision of services to the people of Canada and particularly those services in the field of health and education which are so essential to our survival as a nation. I would urge upon the minister that he proceed as rapidly as possible with the implementation of the hospital plan and that he consider it as merely the first instalment on an over-all health plan to provide for the health needs of every man, woman and child in Canada.

Just before the minister speaks, Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words on the need for further research in two important fields. One of the major health problems confronting Canadians and people everywhere today is cancer. All of us, I am sure, personally know people who have died of cancer and, as individuals, I am sure we continually worry about the question of lung cancer. I would like the minister to tell us what research has been done by the federal government into the question of lung cancer and what the results of that research have been.
Another illness into which some research should be conducted is silicosis. In my part of the country where miners are working in hard rock we are continually plagued with the problem of silicosis. No doubt some hon. members have read in recent months that the incidence of silicosis is dropping very rapidly. The Ontario provincial government on a number of occasions has been asked to investigate this situation and it has established clinics and hospitals capable of dealing with the illness but I do not think the question of basic research into the problem of silicosis has been touched.
In my own area a number of years ago the McIntyre mine established a medical foundation for investigating this condition and they experimented with the prevention of contagion through the inhalation of aluminum dust.
It is quite true that in the hard rock mining areas that have an incidence of silica dust the rate of known silicosis has dropped quite extensively; but the miners and the people in those communities are very fearful. We are told-and this comes not from the Canadian government but from governments across the world, including the governments of Australia, Germany, South Africa and many of the other federal and national governments which have done research into this situation-that the only cure for silicosis is the prevention of silica dust in the air and that can only be accomplished by proper ventilation. I am not suggesting that our people in Canada are not worth as much as people in some of the other countries where they have this problem but I do not think we have been facing up to it.
In the years they have been mining the mining communities have spent very little on ventilation. They have been told that

the research work which the McIntyre foundation did on silicosis is preventing silicosis at the present time. The miners do not agree with that. You can go into Kirkland Lake, Timmins, Noranda, Val D'Or, or any of the northern mining communities, and you will see men 50 years of age who can hardly walk down the street because of the difficulties they have in getting their breath. I would suggest that part of this problem is due to the fact that we have added to the dust in their lungs the aluminum dust that is put into the air. You might say that this is not a matter that affects the Canadian government, but I suggest that research has to be done in this field because the same problem is affecting miners from the Yellowknife and Northwest Territories and every province in Canada where there is a silica problem.
The aluminum dust is added to the other dusts that we breathe both in the mines and on the streets of the towns and to that is added the industrial dusts. To these regular dusts, you add aluminum dust. It is true that when you examine the X-ray plates they do not show clear-cut silicosis. They may show an aggravation of tuberculosis, or they may show nothing at all, but we are finding that these people are having more and more difficulty year by year in breathing and in getting blood circulation to take its proper course. They are dying very young, but their death certificates do not say "silicosis" which is a compensatory disease; they show heart trouble or some of the other pulmonary diseases which are not compensatory. I am suggesting-and it has been suggested by people more capable than I-that the aluminum dust which these mining companies are adding is increasing the problem. It is not a case of whether you want to take the treatment; you have to take it if you work in those communities.
Some hon. members may not know how this is done. In a mining operation there will be a dry room. That is a place where you hang up your clothes. You take off your good clothes in one place and you go to another room where you put on your work clothes and in this room there are a number of air lines and in those air lines they insert a small can of aluminum powder. Under pressure this aluminum powder is blown into the air and anybody walking through that air absorbs into his lungs, a certain percentage of the aluminum dust.
When we have discussed this problem with doctors who are supposed to be experts in this field and have asked them to show

us an X-ray plate which has such an accumulation of aluminum that it would be compensatory-and remember, in Germany alu-minosis is a compensatory disease the same as silicosis is in our country-they have informed us they have never seen X-ray plates that had that amount of aluminum dust indicated on them. I suggest these people are taking this as a prophylactic treatment. Many of them are under the opinion that the incidence of silicosis in Canada has not decreased; it has been covered up. I think the federal government should spend more money and time on doing some research in this field. I am sure it would be possible to get X-ray plates from Germany and other countries that are paying compensation for aluminosis and in that way we could find out just what we are doing to the Canadian people when we fill their lungs full of aluminum dust rather than air. We find that the mortality rate among miners working in hard rock mines is probably just as high as it was a number of years ago. We are also finding, unfortunately, that these people are restricted in getting the compensation that would be their right under the treatment that they are now being compelled to take whether they wish to take it or not.
I also think the Canadian government should do some research into the matter of compulsory portable pensions, particularly for the basic industries of mining and lumbering. We know that the wealth of Canada probably depends to a much greater extent on the health and welfare of our Canadian people than it does on any other single commodity we have and therefore I think we should, if we can, implement an industrial type of pension plan which would allow those people to retire before they have reached the very end of the road. Then we would probably have something to help them along.
Another matter that should be studied very extensively by the Department of National Health and Welfare is nutrition. It is true that in Canada we eat as much as we wish. In the main we are not a hungry nation but we can all remember what happened at the beginning of the war. We were surprised at the vast number of people who tried to enlist for service in that war and were turned down because they were suffering from what the authorities at that time called malnutrition. In my part of the country, northern Ontario, we have both Indian and Eskimo populations. They do not live in my particular riding, but in the vicinity and they are undoubtedly suffering from malnutrition because their diets are not balanced by any stretch of the imagination. Something should
Supply-Health and Welfare be done to assist those people to get the right type of nutrition when they are young so that they will have better teeth and better health in later years.
A few minutes ago one hon. member said something about a health insurance program -the wish is father to the thought-a hospital insurance program in Ontario. From my own observations, since Premier Frost made the declaration that Ontario would embark on a hospitalization plan, I have not seen any great addition to hospitals taking place in the province of Ontario. I am sure the same thing will happen in Ontario that happened in other provinces. We do not need to wait until the hospitals are built. We need a hospitalization plan and once we get that, the hospitals will get built that much sooner. The sooner the federal government gives an impetus to the hospital insurance plan the sooner will it come to pass in Ontario.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few remarks. I will be quite brief. Personally, I want to express my admiration and appreciation of the work done by the staff in this most important department. When my wife and I visited England last summer I had the opportunity to see some of this type of work being done by authorities under the municipal, county, and government of Great Britain. On a number of occasions people with knowledge of what was being done in Canada made very complimentary references to the work being done by the staff of the Department of National Health and Welfare in this country.
In order to save time may I say that I support wholeheartedly the remarks made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, that great champion of health insurance, welfare and the needs of labouring people, the underprivileged and every underdog in the country. I also want to say that I think there is a great need for increased grants in aid for the construction of hospitals. The present grant of $1,000 a bed is completely insufficient under present conditions. I was very pleased to hear the hon. member for York South make some reference to the present situation being a betrayal of the needs of the people at this time. I urge that some consideration be given to this matter.
Prior to coming to this larger sphere of activity-I am not sure of whether it is of influence as far as I am concerned-I was for 20 years a member of a hospital board. I can remember that when we opened our hospital years ago I had the pleasure of taking the present prime minister of Great Britain through the hospital and showing him all its magnificent equipment and

Supply-Health and Welfare modern up-to-date arrangements. I think there were three bedrooms with three beds and six chairs. He was then Captain Harold Macmillan of the Grenadier or Coldstream Guards-I am not sure which-and he was military aide de camp to the Duke of Devonshire. Anyway I will not forget that on that occasion the Duke of Devonshire and Captain Macmillan had occasion to make short speeches and they really patted us on the back. Ever since that time I have been most interested in hospitals.
I do urge that serious consideration be given to increasing these grants. There is a growing need and increasing difficulties are being experienced by local hospital boards and authorities. I am confident that only through the government increasing the grant can we be assured of getting the hospital beds that are required.
I shall make a brief reference to another question. I had occasion recently to have two of the department's publications come over my desk and I was very pleased to get them both. One is a synopsis of the services for the aged in Canada, issued by the research division of the department. I think it is a most excellent synopsis of what is being done by the department and I suggest that any member who is interested in obtaining a good synopsis of the history of the matter and the legislation that the department administers should get a copy of the document. The other one is a synopsis of planning for the aged in Canada issued by the director of the research division of the department. I received it in response to a query as to what was being done with regard to studies in connection with the aged so far as the department is concerned. I would also recommend that members who are interested in this question secure a copy of the document from the research division of the department.
That brings me to another point. I noticed that recently the first Ontario conference on aging was held and I mention it because I have always been very interested in the question. I have seen so many people spend a good number of their latter years without any real enjoyment and in many cases quite unnecessarily because of lack of proper diet or in some cases minor medical or hospital treatment. I was very pleased to see that such a conference had been held and I just want to mention its two main objectives. They are set out in an article in the December issue of Canadian Labour published by the Canadian Labour Congress.
The two main objectives of the conference were: (1) to find out what the problems of the aging in Ontario actually were, and how to go about finding

solutions for them, and (2) to provide an opportunity for those working in this field to learn of each other's activities and discuss coordinated plans for the future.
The program was designed to cover five main aspects of aging: (1) Cost of living and retirement income; (2) Housing and living arrangements: (3) Community services; (4) Employment, unemployment and retirement; and (5) Care, treatment and rehabilitation in hospitals and homes.
I think the agenda of the conference and its purposes were very well organized and I suggest that the Department of National Health and Welfare should use all its influence to get this sort of work going in other provinces and supply whatever assistance it can. I am sure if we get a sufficient number of people to understand the problem and secure co-operation at the local level our provincial and federal plans to assist our older folks, as I like to call them rather than senior citizens, will be very much advanced and improved.
I am tempted by the somewhat tempestuous remarks, shall I say, of the hon. member for London, on the occasion of his first speech in the house, to mention a letter that I received this morning indicating what needs to be done yet in order to care properly for the requirements of our older folks. Incidentally I thought the hon. member took a rather boastful approach to the situation. I believe in giving credit where it is due. The present government has done some worth-while things during its short time in office and I give them credit for it but it must be remembered that the work that has been done is laid on foundations established by the previous government over a great many years-
