The first matter I wish to draw to the attention of the committee is in relation to the building in Ontario of a number of new homes for the aged and the difficulty these people have in recovering the sales tax refund through the channels, I believe, of the Department of National Revenue. I should like to put on the record an analysis of the situation made last January by the then hon. member for Port Arthur, Mr. Howe. In referring to this matter he said:
The trouble seems to lie in the fact that section 47 of the Excise Tax Act was never really intended to apply to the construction of new institutions. It is worded in such a way as to make it clear that it is intended to deal essentially with institutions that are already in existence and that are operating on the basis of a clearly established policy.
Then Mr. Howe went on to state how the institution qualifies and he wound up with this statement:
Supply-Health and Welfare
It would appear that the only solution to this problem may be to obtain an amendment to the Excise Tax Act. Changes in this act are now being considered-
And he completes the letter.
I understand from the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance that there has been no question of bringing in this amendment yet. I gather also from this file of correspondence that Mr. Cecile of the Ontario government has been in touch with the minister's department in connection with this matter. I just want to impress upon him that we should like to have that change made. What I mean is this. The sales tax for Port Arthur undoubtedly will be coming through. But there are going to be a number of these institutions. Our sister city is planning one. There is no reason at all why they should have to wait so long in order to get this refund and to have such difficulty about certification. This point needs to be especially made because at the present time our new home for the aged is embroiled in a controversy with our local council over this matter and it would have a much better financial position to express at the present time if it had had this sales tax refund in connection with building the institution.
The other two matters I wanted to speak about relate to physical fitness and to sport. As the minister is aware, I know, during the last war there was developed a tremendous concern about physical fitness in this country. An act was implemented that was under the jurisdiction of the former minister and there was a physical fitness division which was designed to give grants to the provinces and generally to stimulate physical fitness. A couple of years ago that just sort of petered out and as I understand it the physical fitness division in the old concept has gone. In looking at the debates at the time when the physical fitness division was disappearing, I find that the general attitude of the house seemed to be that this was legislation that did not work, that there did not seem to be any great need for it. In the interim we have had such series as a very responsible newspaper like the Montreal Gazette has been running recently on physical fitness of Canadians and analysing it from the point of view of the tremendous changes in our society that have created a softness and a slackness in us -through the motor car and other developments like that-that cry for a real physical fitness program in the nation.
We happen to have in Canada a great expert on physical fitness, namely Lloyd Per-cival, who every week for many years has put on a program on the C.B.C. I believe he has had over 500 programs now. It is designed for youngsters and young boys. There

Supply-Health and Welfare has been a tremendous response to that program. He has had several hundred thousand letters. There have been some disturbing conclusions from his correspondence and from his investigations. I would suggest that it might be a good idea if the minister in this particular regard consult with Mr. Percival and get some sort of assurance from him. After all, he is a man who is in touch with this particular field and we seem to be lagging behind.
From a personal point of view, my hobby happens to be the history of sports in Canada. In tracing through the trouble that sports such as hockey and lacrosse have fallen on in the last 25 or 30 years we see there has been a tremendous switch in our whole attitude toward leisure. While there are some magnificent developments in the field of hunting, fishing and that sort of thing that are giving our people a real opportunity to exploit the great out of doors that we have, the fact remains that in straight physical terms we do not seem to be developing enough tough and fit people. Perhaps we can look around the house and see examples of that. Perhaps we can look at ourselves. I know the Minister of Transport has a good idea of somehow creating a small gymnasium right in the House of Commons, on the theory that we are going to continue to have more and more young members, these young keen men especially on the far side. If we had a bicycle machine and some weight lifting equipment here we might stave off a few of these heart attacks and perhaps start at this problem right at the heart of the nation, or we like to think that it is the heart of it.
The problem of physical fitness is not one that you can legislate. It comes in from many directions. It is extremely complicated. But surely the national department that embraces this matter has a responsibility that the minister could well take an interest in. I know, as soon as he does begin to take an interest in it the kind of criticism he is going to encounter. So many people, conscious of the tax dollar, look at it as a very frivolous thing on which to spend money. It does not seem so frivolous if we are as conscious of the Russian threat as we like to think we are. There is a tremendous interest now in improving our educational set-up, especially in scientific fields. Yet if any of you have ever oeen associated with war you have to recognize that physical fitness is the final and deciding factor in so many cases, especially in any sort of war or struggle where you have to hold ground. At the present time our young people seem to be lacking in physical fitness and certainly our middleage people in many cases are not examples to them.

Moving on from that to another aspect of physical fitness brings me into the very touchy field of sport and international sport. In Canada there is a tremendous desire amongst the people as a whole that our sporting representatives at Olympic games, empire games and any sort of team sports with which we are associated with the rest of the world we should do better. There is almost an inferiority complex which has developed in relation to the United States in this regard. If one goes back in our Canadian sporting history to before the turn of the century he will find that Canadians can be extremely proud about their heritage in that regard. Up until the late 1890's Canada used to dominate most of the sporting relationships she had with the United States. Canadians took a great deal of pride in it. I believe over $50,000 were bet on Ned Hanlan back in the 1880's when he was rowing away over in Australia. There was great concern.
All these things go to build up national pride. We saw a reflection of this when our hockey team, several years ago, took a defeat and so many people throughout the country took it as a national disaster. You have seen the recent reaction to the rather victorious Russian hockey visit. We are hurt, although we try to be good sports about it, that this thing has developed. This may seem extraneous and far away from the minister's estimates. But sooner or later if we are going to take our position in the international sporting world there must be recognition by the national government that we have a greater responsibility than we have taken in the past. There is no reason why our lacrosse teams and our other teams going abroad should perform in such a slip-shod fashion, why we should send such unfit teams and why, in the training preparatory to the games at all times, our teams have to have such makeshift arrangements.
Now in Toronto, private enterprise-with which your party is so proud to identify itself-has been doing a good job, largely sparked by the people connected with the Canadian national exhibition and there are some very promising results, but there just is not sufficient interest developed until the games are actually taking place. I think that is another aspect which the officials and the minister might keep in mind. I am sure he is not planning and will not plan to do anything about it immediately, but it does seem to me that is worthy of consideration by his department and that strenuous effort should be made to improve the prestige of this nation which means so much to us all in the

international sporting field by enlightened government support of the various facets of sport.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, first of all I would like to join with all those who have said very kind words about the officials of this department. I walked into the office at the corner of Bank and Slater on the afternoon of August 22 and I had to inquire as to where those offices were. I had had no idea previously as I had never been in them before but I soon found myself being made feel very much at home and the assistance given to me at that time and which is still given to me today, for I am certainly very much in the learning stage, has been tremendous. I just could not have gone along without the excellent help of the splendid members of my staff.

subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
There are one or two questions which I think I might clear up as I go along. The hon. member for Port Arthur mentioned sales tax refunds to county homes. I would like to thank the hon. member for mentioning that subject. However, we do now certify to the Department of National Revenue on these sales tax refunds and I think it is on our certifications that action is taken. Now whether the delay is in our department or not I could not say, although I do not think it can be. When we are asked to certify, the information goes out immediately and I do not think we could be considered responsible for delay. I would also like to thank the hon. member for his remarks concerning physical fitness. I would point out that in my department we have a physical fitness consultant on the staff.
The member for Kootenay West also very kindly mentioned my staff. I might mention that the hospital construction grants, which have been mentioned by several members, are being studied, but that is all I can say in that connection.
With respect to the recent old age increase of $9, several members have mentioned that subject and I have seen newspaper items in this connection. I think all we can do is say that the cheque goes to the recipient. Certainly we give the increase to the beneficiary mentioned. While I am assuming it is the business of county home organizations, or whoever may be concerned with matters of this type, as to what they do about raising rents, at the same time I personally would be very disappointed if the beneficiary did not receive some additional amount as a result of the $9 increase.
The member for Timiskaming made some very helpful suggestions. I would point out
Supply-Health and Welfare to him with respect to cancer research, however, that prior to 1948-1949 the fundamental research on cancer was limited in Canada due to lack of facilities, senior research personnel and assured long-term support. Although national research council did allocate grants for short-term projects, applications received were not commensurate to the extent of the problem to stimulate and co-ordinate basic research. The national research council was established in 1947. Research increased rapidly and in 1948 to 1949 projects totalling 25 were started. In 1954 to 1955, 78 projects as well as 14 research fellowships were started. For 1956 to 1957 the total was 81 awards granted involving some $540,000 in addition to 17 research fellowships for a total value of $65,000. In 1956 to 1957 roughly 70 per cent of the money was provided by the Canadian cancer society and most of the remaining 30 per cent was provided by federal-provincial grants. In all, over the past nine years, a total of $900,000 has been provided in support of research through the health grants program, with an equal amount from provincial sources. It is quite an extensive program and it has been growing very rapidly.
The hon. member also mentioned silicosis and I understand that the provincial authorities actually do look after this matter but we have and will upon request make surveys. I also understand we have made a survey in Nova Scotia and I am not sure about the others but I will be happy to look into that question.
The member for Montmagny-L'Islet asked if I was going to have any increased or further supplementary estimates-

subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Additional.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Additional, yes. There will be some for Hungarian immigration medical and a transfer to do whatever is necessary for old age security.

subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: But not for family allowances.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
No transfer to the old age security fund.
There have been several suggestions about hospital insurance and I may come to them a little later-

subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Would the minister answer my brief question at this time?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Yes, I am not proposing any reductions in the estimates at this time. I do not doubt that the department might be able to find some savings somewhere along the line and I am hoping to keep a close eye on that but I am not making any motion for reduction.

Supply-Health and Welfare

subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman did not quite understand my question. It was not what he thought but what the Minister of Finance thought. The minister boasted several times that he had found extravagances.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Well, you ask the Minister of Finance about that, will you?

subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Oh, I will.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
The member for Medicine Hat inquired concerning certain matters which he considered were problems. Yes, there are some problems having to do with hospital insurance and I will come back to those in a moment.
The member for Burin-Burgeo inquired as to travelling clinics. I might mention that there has been $20,000 approved this year for a radio telephone service based on St. Anthony, Newfoundland, extending the service into Labrador. If an approach is received for a similar service on the four south coast boats already operating by the grant we will certainly be glad to look into the matter.
The hon. member also inquired as to deratization services. This matter has been brought to my attention and I will be happy to look into it and consider the matter further.
The hon. member for Comox-Alberni felt that possibly I should have made an opening statement. I do not see any particular benefit which would have been derived by my doing that. I should like to point out that five pieces of legislation have gone through the house under my sponsorship, with one more at least to come, and these have provided a fairly busy period. He said that probably a new broom might sweep clean. I think I mentioned when I first stood up that I had a particularly good staff. I am certainly finding that the department is well run. There may be some changes; I mentioned in a previous debate I was going to give consideration to a lot of things, such as the regulations under the disability act- a more considered study than possibly has been made for some little time. I have a lot of these things to look into when the house rises and I find the odd moment in which to do it.

subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, when I referred to sweeping with a broom I was not referring to sweeping out some of the staff; I was referring to sweeping out some of the dusty policies of the previous administration.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I intend to do some of that too. The hon. member for Winnipeg North

Centre mentioned specifically the six provinces, and went on to inquire what we were going to do in this respect. All I can say is what the Prime Minister said at the opening of the dominion-provincial conference:
Unless you express strong reasons to the contrary we are inclined now to recommend to parliament a change in the law to remove the "six provinces" clause and to substitute for it an earlier and more definite date for commencement of the plan.
That legislation is to go before the house as announced.
The hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke was concerned about research, and mental health research particularly. Our total research program this year for mental research amounts to over $500,000. That figure has grown tremendously over the years.
I rather think, Mr. Chairman, that covers most of the specific questions asked, except that there were many statements and questions put with regard to the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act. I should like to assure the hon. member for Essex East that I am firmly of the belief that this act is going to be operative in Canada earlier than it would have been if he had still been holding this office. I believe that very definitely. We have been accused by several hon. members of delay. I do not feel there is any justification for that statement whatsoever. The act was passed-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Then show us the evidence.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: It was the hon. member's opinion that there has been delay. It is my opinion that there has not been any delay.

subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: How about a few facts?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I am going to give you a few facts. The act was passed in 1957-it was proclaimed on May 1-and the draft forms of agreement were circulated for study together with the draft regulations. Teams of officials visited all the provinces in the course of last summer expressing desire to discuss the bill.
The dominion-provincial conference was held late in November. In the meantime there was discussion back and forth between provincial and federal officials, and then a technical conference was called for December 11, 12 and 13. Technical officials were invited to this conference from all the provinces and I may point out that representatives came from all provinces with the exception of Alberta. By the way, during the dominion-provincial conference I had discussions with the minister from Manitoba, the minister from Alberta and the minister from British

Columbia. I also had a short conversation with the premier of Saskatchewan. I have had conversations with representatives of Ontario, also, and I should like to point out that while Alberta was the only province refusing to come to the dominion-provincial technical conference early in December, I think possibly that province would have benefited if representatives had attended. At that time, many differences of opinion were ironed out, though there are one or two still outstanding. We think the act is administratively possible the way it is. I realize that there has possibly been some disagreement about that, but I do feel this last conference ironed out practically all the difficult points.
I should like to conclude at this point by stating that all the steps necessary toward the implementation of the hospital insurance act have been going forward. It is certainly going to be in operation and the provinces will be receiving federal grants, as the Prime Minister stated in the conference, "at an earlier and more definite date". I do not think I have anything further to say on the matter, but if there are any questions I shall be glad to deal with them.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Did
the minister not take note of the remarks made regarding mental and tubercular hospitals?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Yes, I have. I could say this. It stands exactly where it stood when I was asked a question a short time ago, I think. At any rate it is a matter of government policy and at this moment I am not stating what is going to happen.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Would the minister accept a question now on this point?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: may say that I do not have on my desk at the moment the record of the open session of the federal-provincial conference but as I recall it the Prime Minister made a statement that day with regard to mental and tubercular hospitals similar to the one he made about the six-province requirement. In other words, up until that time the government and the Conservative party seemed willing to go ahead with the idea of including mental and tubercular hospitals in this legislation but as the minister knows there is no record of what was said at the federal-provincial conference the next day.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
But there was quite a divergence of opinion later on the opening day.
Supply-Health and Welfare

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Was
it a divergence of opinion that changed the government's mind on this matter?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: No, I would not say that. I would simply say there was not unanimity of opinion as there was regarding the six-provinces provision.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Since the minister is talking about what happened on Monday, November 25-in other words I will not ask him what happened in the secret session-will he tell us which provinces expressed a desire for any change in the position?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: It is in the record of the proceedings of the open session of the conference.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
The
minister has his copy on his desk and I do not have mine here. He can answer the question.

subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Before the minister answers that question, if the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre will permit my putting a further question, I would ask this. Is this not the situation: the Prime Minister at the dominion-provincial conference announced that the government proposed to include tuberculosis and mental illness in the hospital insurance act thereby committing the federal government to sharing with the provinces the cost of these two coverages under that act, but that the Prime Minister, in contradiction of what he had said during the course of the election and what he had urged along with others when they were in opposition, said that those inclusions would take place but that any money spent by the federal government with respect to these two inclusions representing an estimated expenditure of some $68 million would be deducted from any further grants made under the fiscal agreements. Some of the provinces who were anxious to have mental illness and tuberculosis included were not perpared to accept that particular proposal. Is that not the situation?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I am sorry, but I was examining the record of the dominion-provincial conference to see what the Prime Minister actually said on that day. As I understand the hon. member for Essex East he is suggesting that the amount which might be required to implement the inclusion of mental and tubercular hospitals would be reduced from any additional amount which might be given to the provinces?

subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Yes.

Supply-Health and Welfare

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I think it is only reasonable to expect that that would happen. An amount of $70 million or so cannot be tossed around casually, you know.

subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: It was tossed around during the election, though.

subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: But that was not the question put by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. He simply asked if it was not a fact that the government had announced at the dominion-provincial conference a change of policy and that mental illness and tuberculosis would be included and that gave rise to much hope.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: If there was unanimity.

subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I do not think the Prime Minister said "if there was unanimity". I may be wrong in that particular but in that context I do not think he used those words. In any event if tuberculosis and mental illness were included the amount given by the federal government for those two coverages would be deducted from any increase in further grants made pursuant to the fiscal agreements.
That is not what the Prime Minister said during the course of the election. That is not what hon. gentlemen opposite when in opposition said should be done and said they would do if they were given a chance to bring forward legislation. What I am saying is that having given these assurances during the election and having made these demands when in opposition the government, apart altogether from what may be the financial merits in themselves, could not reasonably take the position which the Prime Minister did take and-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: You are so wrong.

subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The minister tells me that I am wrong. He always says that but he does not indicate in what particular I am wrong.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I will tell you in a moment.

subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
What is going to happen? The province of Ontario is now making its preparations for its particular scheme and included in that is an insurance arrangement under its plan for tuberculosis and mental illness with a designated premium, I think, of 25 cents. Ontario does not want any change with regard to tuberculosis or mental illness. It wants to get all the money it can out of the federal government, something in the neighbourhood of $100 million. That will also be the attitude of the province of Quebec. And when Ontario gets that money in a subsequent period it will come back to the government and ask that
[Mr. Martin (Essex East) .1
the federal government provide grants under the hospital insurance act to cover those two illnesses. That is the position in which the government has put itself as a result of going back on the promise it made to the Canadian people.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: It has not gone back on it.

subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: My hon. friend says that the government has not gone back on its promise.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: It has gone back on none of its promises.

subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I would like to hear the minister explain in a reasonable manner that the government intends to include tuberculosis and mental illness without any conditions, and assure us that the conditions I have envisaged will not arise.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I am not going to say what is definitely going to happen. I am only going to explain what the Prime Minister said at the conference. He used the following words on that occasion:
My colleagues and I have no objection in principle to introducing amendments in parliament to provide for inclusion of mental hospitals and tuberculosis sanatoria which have been estimated will cost $68 million to begin with if all the provinces come in and the cost will mount year by year but we wish to make clear that whatever is offered to provincial treasurers in this matter cannot be provided in other forms, and in particular must be taken into consideration in any revision that takes place of the Tax Sharing Arrangements Act.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: That is clear.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Now, wait a minute. If there is going to be an adjustment in the tax sharing arrangements act the adjustment could involve $68 million. That is all it amounts to.

subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: It could be that.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: That is all it is.

subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
But I say to my
friend with great respect-and I quite appreciate the difficulties of his position-this could undoubtedly be the case but that is not what the Prime Minister of this country said in the election he would do. He said in Saskatoon on May 27, "the Conservative party still believes that hospital insurance should cover patients in mental and tuberculosis institutions". He said nothing whatever about deducting the amounts of money that this particular policy would involve from the fiscal grants. When he spoke in Massey Hall in Toronto in the presence of the premier of Ontario he indicated then his belief in hospital insurance. He said that those items should be included in that measure at the very meeting when Premier Frost himself, turning to the Prime Minister, said, "Ontario

has not had a fair deal from the federal government in the matter of fiscal grants."

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Nor had it.

subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: There was the man pointing to the Prime Minister who would rectify this situation and give Ontario the $100 million to which he thought that province was entitled.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The figure $100 million was not used.

subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: It was used by Mr. Frost not only at that meeting but at many meetings all over the province of Ontario including one held in the city of London not far from where the hon. gentleman and I live. The people of this country were led to believe that there would be these generous fiscal arrangements and that there would be no deductions from them for any purpose whatsoever. I say to the hon. gentleman-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: You do not know what the ceiling is on fiscal arrangement adjustments.

subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
That may be. The
ceiling is not the point.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Yes, it is.

subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: With great respect, I say no. Suppose the ceiling is only $25 million, not $100 million.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I am not going to get into that.

subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I can well understand why my hon. friend does not want to. Suppose the ceiling is $25 million. What we are saying is that we were told that tubercular and mental illness would be included-

subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Without condition.

subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: -without any condition whatsoever, and the Prime Minister has placed my hon. friend in a very embarrassing and difficult position.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Far from it.

subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
My hon. friend can say "far from it", but the fact is that although his party advocated the inclusion of tubercular and mental illness, they are not now prepared to take that step in accordance with their promises made in the election campaign. They have added a reservation that was never present and which was offered, I am sure, after they were confronted with the financial situation in which they have got themselves and for which they must accept full responsibility.
Supply-Health and Welfare

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the exchange between the hon. member for Essex East and the Minister of National Health and Welfare reminds me- and I mention it to make my point-of the reverse of the situation that we had here last spring. On that occasion it was the member for Essex East who was sitting over on the other side as the minister. He was annoyed at what he regarded as delay in connection with the passing of the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Did you say the minister was annoyed? Oh, that one, yes.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The annoyance of the present minister reminds me of the annoyance of the former minister when the present Minister of Finance, as the member for Eglinton, moved an amendment to third reading of the bill calling for the inclusion of mental and tubercular hospitals.

subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Without any deductions.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Without any deductions; no strings attached. It was a matter of principle. Those who were here will recall the strong speech made by the present Prime Minister, who was then the leader of the opposition, and who urged that illness was illness whether it was physical or mental, and that it was a disgraceful thing the former Liberal government was doing by failing to include mental and tubercular hospitals within the four corners of this legislation. That was the position the Conservatives took. I realize that the minister did not take part in that debate-his interests were in other subjects in those days-but his colleagues did. They took the position very strongly that as a matter of right and as a matter of principle mental and tubercular illnesses should be included with other illnesses in this particular legislation.
My hon. friend, the hon. member for Essex East, has already referred to the stand taken in the campaign. He quoted from what the Prime Minister said at Saskatoon and referred to what he said at Toronto. Let us look at the report of his speech in another of our major cities which will make it clear. According to the Winnipeg Tribune of May 14, 1957, the Prime Minister said that:
The Conservatives would repair a "serious omission" in the federal health plan which does not include tubercular and mental institutions.
There was no question about it last session; there was no question about it during the election campaign, where the Tories stood. They stood for the inclusion of mental and
2756	HOUSE OF
Supply-Health and Welfare tubercular institutions. I go further, Mr. Chairman. Along with their stand on mental and tubercular institutions, they took a similar stand regarding the removal of the six-province requirement.
Let us get down to this present session. As has already been pointed out, at the start of the session there was silence on the part of the government regarding hospital insurance; but in response to questions on the orders of the day and in response to our presenting a motion of no confidence on this matter, statements got made. Mr. Chairman, up until Monday, November 25, statements made by the government on these two issues, the removal of the six-province requirement and the bringing in of mental and tuberculosis hospitals, were on the same plane. They were both matters that the government was prepared to consider; they were both matters the government was prepared to discuss with the provinces; they were both matters the government was prepared to put on the agenda of the federal-provincial conference that met on November 25 and 26.
I come now to November 25. The Prime Minister said to the federal-provincial conference that the government had no objection in principle to making these two changes, but as the hon. member for Essex East has pointed out, one of them that day for the first time had a string attached to it; namely the inclusion of mental and tubercular hospitals. Therefore, as has been pointed out, some difference of opinion arose amongst the provinces on that day. I confess some of us wonder whether the string was put there deliberately so that one or more of the provinces would take a second look at this proposition. As a result of that, as a result of what happened on Monday, November 25, we have had a different picture ever since. Since that time the willingness to withdraw the six-province requirement still stands. It gets mentioned every once in a while when we ask questions about it or have occasion to do so. But this matter of including mental and tubercular hospitals has now become one of those mysterious matters of government policy on which no statement can be made. Why the difference? Why is it that both of these matters were on the same plane and treated in the same way up to November 25, but since then, one of them is something about which there is going to be legislation, namely the removal of the six-province requirement, but the other is one of those mysterious matters about which there has to be an announcement of government policy if and when the government considers taking up the matter. Mr. Chairman, it looks very clear to some of us as though this whole idea that the Conservatives made the subject of an amendment to


the third reading of the bill last spring, which the Conservatives made so much of during the election campaign, which the Conservatives took to the federal-provincial conference, has been droped so far as this government is concerned.
We contend, Mr. Chairman, that that is a betrayal of election promises, a betrayal of commitments made to the people and of the stand they took in this house during last spring and that they had better consider this very seriously before it breaks them altogether.
There has been an announcement made that there will be legislation to remove the six-province requirement. I do not know why this has not been introduced before this. Other items not as important have reached the order paper. Why has not this one been put on the order paper? But since it has not been put on the order paper it gives the government a chance, when it does bring down those proposed amendments to the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act, to include in the amendment two provisions, one the removal of the six-province requirement and the other the inclusion of mental and tubercular hospitals. I call upon this government, if it wants the Canadian people to have any confidence in the stand it took when it was in opposition, if it wants the people to have any confidence in its election promises, to get back on the rails so far as this important issue is concerned.

Mr. Speaker, it will not be necessary for me to ask the house leader what the business is for the session when we reconvene because he has already given that, but I do want to take this opportunity to tell the house leader how happy I have been on this side of the house to be associated with him in the business of the house in the last two months. I assure him it has been a pleasure to me to work with him in this entirely new position so far as I am concerned, and I should like him to know that the relationship has been very pleasant.
I should also like to extend to him and those associated with him on the other side of the house our very best wishes for Christmas and the new year with the hope that in the new year he will be able to give us in advance at least one week's business. I should also like to add that I hope the new year for him and those associated with him will be a most happy one in all aspects save the field of public life. I venture to hope that during the course of 1958 it will be possible for the house leader and myself to exchange positions.
I would not want to leave this happy note without telling you, Mr. Speaker, how happy we on this side of the house have been to have you preside over the destinies of parliament. You have done a magnificent job. I am sure all of us on this side would want me to say that you have performed your duties fairly and equitably, always keeping in mind the decorum that should exist in the house, and particularly in presiding over the welfare of this assembly with great equity as you have done. I should like to repeat the sentiments I have expressed to the house leader and pass them on to you and wish you a very merry Christmas and the most happy new year.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I join with the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier), speaking on behalf of the members of this group, in wishing the season's best greetings to all our colleagues in parliament, on all sides of the house. May I also have the very real pleasure of joining with the hon. member for Laurier in the expressions that he made to yourself, Mr. Speaker. He put it very well. We have enjoyed greatly your work as the presiding officer of this house. Your good sense and your sense of humour have been invaluable. It is indeed a pleasure for us to wish to you and Mrs. Michener a very merry Christmas and a happy new year.

Mr. Speaker, 1 said on the first day of the session that your good self was a very proper person for the very exalted position you now occupy, very largely because you were born in Alberta where our people have all those qualities that make good Speakers. We have appreciated your fairness and the splendid way in which you have conducted the business of the house. We are not at all disappointed with what you have done. I want to join with all the others in wishing to all our colleagues a very merry Christmas and for the year 1958 an abundance of all those good things that human beings enjoy.
